messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text: Sefa shifts her weight and folds her arms, the prayer beads clicking softly at her wrist. "Three questions before we step out, Master Vell. How did Jassan die, and has his room been opened since? What does this seal look like, so we can know a whole one from one that's been picked at? And the key to the strongbox—does it stay with him, or is it here?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell leans an elbow on the counter, not quite touching the clerk's tidy desk, and takes Vell in the way he'd take in a lock — unhurried.

"A few things, Master Vell, since it's our necks on the Coast Way and not yours." He counts them off on his fingers, mirroring Vell's tapping. "One: what does this box look like? Size, iron or wood, whose seal is on it — yours or Ferr's? I'd hate to carry home the wrong one. Two: who holds the key to that room now? The cooper, a landlady, the Fist? If the door's locked and the owner's absent, I'll want to know whether I'm *allowed* in or merely *expected* to be." He lets that sit a heartbeat. "Three: who else knows the box is there and wants it? A man doesn't pay seventy-five gold for a stroll down the road to fetch a parcel. And four—" his voice drops a little, "how did Jassan Ferr die? Fever, drink, or did somebody help him along? It matters to how carefully I open his door."

He glances sideways at Sefa and Bram, then back. "Answer straight and we're gone inside the quarter-hour."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I rest my hand on my sword’s pommel, leaving it sheathed.

“Three days dead, and you’re hiring three of us to fetch a box a short walk away. What killed Jassan, and is anyone likely to dispute your claim?”

I nod toward the ledgers behind Vell. “We’ll also need a description of the box and its seal, and a written order for whoever keeps the rooms. Rather not break a cooper’s door over an honest errand.”

I watch Vell as he answers, particularly when he speaks of Jassan.

screens.Bram Halloway:
Sefa folds her arms, her prayer beads clicking at her wrist, and asks Vell three things: how Jassan died and whether his room has been opened since, what the seal looks like so a whole one can be told from a tampered one, and whether the strongbox key stays with the dead man or is here.

Pell leans an elbow on the counter, close to the clerk's desk but not touching it, and studies Vell the way a locksmith studies a lock. He counts off questions on his fingers: what the box looks like (its size, whether it is iron or wood, and whose seal it bears, Vell's or Ferr's); who holds the key to the room now, and whether the three of you would be allowed in or only expected to go in; who else knows about the box and might want it, given the seventy-five gold on offer; and how Jassan Ferr died. He adds that if Vell answers straight, you will be gone within the quarter-hour.

Vell lets all of you finish. He doesn't interrupt and he doesn't hurry. When Pell stops counting, Vell puts his finger back on the counter.

"His heart." The finger taps once. "Wenna Pike found him in the morning. She keeps the rooms over the cooper's yard. A brother came down from the Song of the Morning and said it was his heart. Nobody helped him. Who would help a clerk die?" His eyes go briefly to the window and the hammering outside, then back. "Wenna has the key to the room. I haven't been inside. I have a counter to keep."

He has said nothing yet about the box, its seal, or a written order.

scenes.narration:
Vell lets them finish. He doesn't interrupt and he doesn't hurry. When Pell stops counting on his fingers, Vell puts his own finger back on the counter.

"His heart." The finger taps once. "Wenna Pike found him in the morning. She keeps the rooms over the cooper's yard. A brother came down from the Song of the Morning and said it was his heart. Nobody helped him. Who would help a clerk die?" His eyes go briefly to the window and the hammering, then back. "Wenna has the key to the room. I haven't been inside. I have a counter to keep."

Bram watches him while he says it, and sees nothing like grief. Vell says "his heart" the way a man repeats something he was glad to hear, and he says it a little too fast, as if a doubt had been answered for him before he could think it. In all the time he talks about Jassan he never once looks at the empty desk beside him. He stops himself from looking, and that is a different thing.

"The box." He holds his hands apart, about a forearm's length. "Oak. Iron at the corners, two drop handles, a brass plate with my name on the lid. One man carries it with both hands." He turns the heavy ring on his right hand so the face shows: a square of dark stone cut with a key between the letters O and V. "My seal. Red wax over the hasp, this mark in it. If it's cracked, smeared or pressed twice, it's been touched. I'll know." He turns the ring back. "The key to the box stays with me. You won't need it."

Pell has watched locks for longer than he has watched men, and this one gives. Vell talks about the ledgers like stock, things to count and nothing more. When he gets to the seal his voice tightens, and he spends more words on it than on everything else together. Whatever he's buying back for seventy-five gold, it isn't paper. It's being able to show someone that nobody has read it.

"Who else wants it." Vell answers this one quickly, as if it were easy. "Gerrit Thale keeps a counting-room down the Way. He'd give a good deal to read my books and steal my clients. He knows Jassan is dead. Everyone in Beregost knows Jassan is dead." He stops there, and Pell notices how readily he gave Thale's name, the way a man offers up the smaller of two worries.

He looks at Bram last. "Why three? Three are harder to rob than one, and harder to buy." He pulls a slip of paper toward him, dips the pen and writes fast in a clerk's hand. He blows on the ink, folds the paper, drips red wax on the fold and presses the ring into it. The key and the O and V stand out clean and sharp. He lays the note on the counter in front of Bram.

"For Wenna Pike. It says the bearers fetch the counting-house's strongbox on my word. If she wants anything else, she can come and ask me for it." He folds his hands again. Out in the street a hammer stops and another one starts up.

 Bram has watched enough men talk across enough wagon-tailboards to read this one, and he does: the death doesn't trouble Vell. What troubles him is how close he came to having to wonder whether it was something else.

Pell gets further. He doesn't learn what is in the box, but he has Vell's measure now. This is a man who already has a buyer waiting for those ledgers, or a judge, and he will pay to put an unbroken seal in front of whoever it is.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell straightens off the counter. He's got what the lock will give him; forcing it further only scratches the plate.

"Oak, iron corners, brass with your name, red wax, key between O and V. Seal whole." He says it back flat, a runner repeating an address. "One more, and then we're gone. Gerrit Thale — does he send men, or does he send coin? A man who sends coin, I'd like to know whether Wenna Pike has had a visitor since the brother from the Song went home." He nods at the sealed note. "If she says no, good. If she says yes, that tells us whether we're walking to a parcel or to an empty room, and I'd rather know on the Coast Way than on your counter at dusk with nothing in our hands."

He doesn't wait long for the answer — he's already turning to the other two, voice lower. "Walk in by the front with the note, Bram, you've got the face for honest errands. Sefa with you; a landlady who's had a death in the house will talk to a woman with beads before she talks to either of us. I'll come in behind and have a look at the room before anyone's hands are on anything — a man's room tells you how he died quicker than a brother from a temple does. And I'll want a look at the back of the cooper's yard. Three days is a long time for a locked box to sit unmolested in a town where everyone knows the clerk's dead."

He gives Vell a short, civil nod. "Before nightfall, Master Vell."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take the note, letting the wax harden before stowing it safely.

“If the seal’s already broken when Wenna opens the door, that’s not our doing. We’ll bring you word rather than pretend otherwise.”

I look to Sefa and Pell. “Ready when you are.”

Once we’re outside and out of Vell’s hearing, I lower my voice. “He wasn’t grieving. Fair enough—not every employer does. But he seemed relieved someone had called it his heart. I’d like to hear what Wenna found.”

I head toward the cooper’s yard with the others, keeping an eye on the street behind us.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the others do the pressing; she stands a little back and watches Vell as he answers, listening less to the words than to the pauses. What he says about the seal and the key sounds precise, the sort of precision that wants to be believed.

When he has finished, she says quietly, "You said a brother came down from Lathander's temple and called it his heart. Did he leave a name, or say why he was so sure?" She glances at Bram and Pell. "And Master Vell—when we bring the box back, will it be only your hands that lift it? Or will someone else be waiting behind that counter with an interest of their own?"

He repeats back the description of the box: oak, iron corners, a brass plate with a name, red wax, a key stamped between an O and a V, the seal whole. He asks Vell whether Gerrit Thale sends men or coin, and whether Wenna Pike has had any visitor since the brother from the temple went home. He says it matters to know whether they are heading for a parcel or for a bare, empty room. Then he turns to you and Bram and lowers his voice. He proposes that Bram go in the front with the note, and that you go with him, since a landlady who has lost a lodger will talk to a woman with beads sooner than to either man. He will follow, look over the room before anyone touches anything, and also check the back of the cooper's yard. He gives Vell a short, civil nod and promises they'll be back before nightfall.

Bram takes the note and lets the wax harden, then tucks it inside his coat. He tells Vell that if the seal is already broken when Wenna opens the door, that won't be the party's doing, and they will bring word of it.

Vell answers Pell first, and quickly. Thale sends coin first, then a man for the rest: Coll Brannock, broad, quiet, with a Gate way of talking. About visitors to Wenna Pike he knows nothing; he says he hasn't been there and that they should ask her. When Bram speaks of a broken seal, Vell's mouth goes thin. He says to bring the box anyway, and to tell him whose hands broke it. He glances at the ring on his own finger and says he will know the wax.

You had asked about the brother from the temple. Vell spreads his fingers on the wood and says Wenna sent up to the temple for him. He didn't ask the man's name; he was a priest, and he said heart, as though that settled it. Then you asked whose hands would lift the box in the end, and whether anyone else would be waiting behind the counter. Vell takes a breath before he answers, and you watch that breath.

Vell draws the breath calmly, as though a ledger had been set down open before him. "Only my hands will lift the box when you bring it here," he says. "And my counter. And my two eyes on the seal." His hands stay folded; his eyes don't flick toward the clerk's desk.

The street's hammering begins again, closer now.

Then she asks whose hands will lift the box at the end, and whether anyone else will be waiting behind the counter. He takes a breath before he answers, and Sefa watches that breath.

"My counter. My hands. Nobody else's business but mine." He says it flatly, the way he said everything else, and Sefa finds nothing behind it. No catch in the voice, no glance at the strongroom door. As far as she can tell, it is a plain answer from a man who has run out of patience with questions. He folds his hands. "Before nightfall."

Outside, the street is all noise and heat from the forges. A smith's boy runs past with a bucket of slack water. Two carters are arguing over a wheel. Bram walks a few steps toward the corner, lowers his voice and says what he thought of Vell: no grief, and something too much like relief that someone had called it his heart. Then he starts down the hill with one eye on the street behind them. Nobody falls in behind. A woman with a basket of eggs, a dog and a Fist trooper yawning in a doorway are all on their own business, and none of them looks twice at three hirelings.

The Coast Way runs west out of the smithy streets, toward the sea. It is quieter here, mostly yards and lodging-houses. After ten minutes they reach the cooper's yard. You smell it first, cut oak and hot iron hoops. A gate of grey planks stands half open on a yard full of stacked staves. A man with leather sleeves is driving a hoop down onto a barrel with steady blows. A wooden stair runs up the outside of the building to a gallery with three doors. The middle shutter on the gallery is closed. The other two are open to the morning.

Pell is a few paces behind the other two, as he meant to be. On the gatepost at hip height, where nobody looks, there is a small chalk mark: a circle with a short stroke through it, fresh enough that the rain hasn't touched it. Anyone from the Wide could read it without stopping. *This house is being watched.*

 Sefa watched that breath for a tell and didn't find one. Whatever sat behind "my counter, my hands" got past her, and she walked out of the counting-house believing Vell had given her a plain, honest answer.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Your plan suits me,” I tell Pell quietly. “We’ll ask before touching anything.”

I step through the gate, staying clear of the cooper’s work, and wait for a pause in his hammering.

“Morning. Looking for Wenna Pike. Bram Halloway—we’ve an order from Ostrin Vell about his clerk’s strongbox. Where might we find her?”

I keep the note tucked away until Wenna herself appears. While we wait, I glance over the gallery and yard for anyone watching our arrival.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stops at the gate, one hand on the grey plank, and looks up at the three doors and the closed middle shutter. The hammering here is not like the smithies' hammers; it is slower, more patient.

She glances at Pell, then at Bram, and keeps her voice low. "The middle one, then. A shutter pulled in close while the other two want the morning air. That will be the dead man's room." She touches the prayer beads once, briefly, out of habit. "Bram, you have the note. Knock lightly and let her look at us before we say anything. I'd rather not put a fright into a woman who has already found one body this week."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops at the gatepost as if to shift his pack, and his thumb finds the chalk mark without looking at it. Circle, stroke through. He's drawn that one himself, on the Wide, more than once. Someone from home has been here, or someone taught by someone from home.

He doesn't rub it out. A rubbed mark tells the chalker someone read it.

He closes the two paces to Bram and Sefa, falling in at Bram's shield shoulder so his mouth is near Bram's ear and his back is to the street. Low, conversational, like a man remarking on the weather: "Gatepost. Chalk. That's a Guild mark, or a good copy — it means *this house is watched, keep clear or report.* Fresh since the last rain. So Thale's man, or somebody else's, has been standing on this street in the last day, and may still be." He lets his eyes drift, not his head: the yards opposite, the lodging-house windows, the lane ends. "Don't look round. Go up with the note like honest folk. Talk to Wenna on the gallery where I can see you, and don't let her open that middle door until I've come up the back — if the shutter's closed but the room's been visited, I want to see the sill before three pairs of boots are on it."

To Sefa, a touch softer: "Ask her if anyone's come asking after Jassan's things. A friend, a cousin, a man with a Gate voice. Watch her hands when she answers, not her face."

Then he peels off, unhurried, as if he's just the third hireling who'd rather have a word with the cooper than climb stairs. He gives the man in the leather sleeves a nod and a "Morning," and walks along the stacked staves toward the back of the yard — looking for the rear of the building under the middle shutter, any lane behind, a drainpipe or the beam-ends he can go up by, and above all for anyone who has the gate in view and no barrel in front of them.

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Bram told you quietly that your plan suited him and that the three of you would ask before touching anything. He went in through the gate, kept clear of the cooper's work, and waited for a break in the hammering. Then he gave his name, said the party had an order from Ostrin Vell about his clerk's strongbox, and asked where Wenna Pike might be found. He kept the note out of sight until Wenna herself should appear, and looked over the gallery and the yard as he waited.

Sefa stopped at the gate with a hand on the grey plank. She looked up at the three doors and the closed middle shutter, and she said quietly that the middle room would be the dead man's. She suggested Bram knock lightly and let the woman look at them before they said anything, so as not to frighten someone who had already found one body this week.

You walked along the stacked staves toward the back of the yard, as if you only wanted a look at good oak. The back of the yard ends at a shed with a lean-to roof. Its eaves come within a few feet of a small back window, which by your reckoning belongs to the middle room. The window's shutter is latched from the inside. Moss grows along the ridge of the lean-to in an even green line, unbroken from end to end. Nobody has walked that roof in a long while. Beyond the shed lies a nettle lane with a ditch in it, and nobody is in sight. From where you stand, the open half of the gate frames a strip of the Coast Way, and you study that strip the way you were taught to on the Wide.

Behind you, Bram's question reached the cooper. The cooper finished his stroke before he looked up. He is a heavy-shouldered man with grey in his beard and a leather sleeve laced on each forearm. He kept his eyes on the barrel's rim while Bram spoke. He gave his name as Tobin and said the yard is his and the rooms are hers. He tipped his head toward a low door under the outside stair, with a bucket and a scrubbing brush on the step, and said she was in and would have heard them. Then he said Vell had not come himself, then, in a tone that asked for no answer, and the hammer came down again.

From the gate you could see the gallery. The left-hand door stands open, with a chair and a pot of thyme outside it. A shirt hangs drying over the rail by the right-hand door. The middle door is shut under its shutter, with a padlock on its hasp. The padlock is new, its brass still bright, and it's the only new thing up there. Across the lane is a chandler's shop under a striped awning. A broad man leans on the awning post with an apple in his hand. A boy sweeps the step, and two doors down a woman beats a rug out of an upper window. Nobody stares at the yard. Everyone is busy with something.

Bram told you quietly that your plan suited him and that the three of you would ask before touching anything. He went in through the gate, kept clear of the cooper's work, and waited for a break in the hammering. Then he gave his name, said the party had an order from Ostrin Vell about his clerk's strongbox, and asked where Wenna Pike might be found. He kept the note out of sight until Wenna herself should appear, and looked over the gallery and the yard as he waited.

Sefa stopped at the gate with a hand on the grey plank. She looked up at the three doors and the closed middle shutter, and she said quietly that the middle room would be the dead man's. She suggested Bram knock lightly and let the woman look at them before they said anything, so as not to frighten someone who had already found one body this week.

You walked along the stacked staves toward the back of the yard, as if you only wanted a look at good oak. The back of the yard ends at a shed with a lean-to roof. From the back of the yard Pell can't tell which.

The kitchen door under the stair opens. A woman of about fifty comes out drying her hands on her apron. She's lean, her sleeves are pushed to the elbow, and a key hangs on a cord at her waist. He is a heavy-shouldered man with grey in his beard and a leather sleeve laced on each forearm. He hears Bram out and keeps his eyes on the barrel's rim the whole time.

"Tobin. The yard's mine, the rooms are hers." He tips his head at a low door under the outside stair, with a bucket and a scrubbing brush on the step beside it. "She's in. She'll have heard you." He sets the driver back on the hoop, then stops. "Vell didn't come himself, then." It isn't a question, and he doesn't wait for an answer. The hammer comes down again.

While Tobin talks, Bram looks the place over. Up on the gallery the left-hand door stands open, with a chair and a pot of thyme outside it. A shirt hangs drying over the rail by the right-hand door. The middle door is shut under its shutter, and a padlock hangs on its hasp. The padlock is new, its brass still bright, and it's the only new thing on the gallery. Across the lane there's a chandler's shop under a striped awning. A broad man leans on the awning post with an apple in his hand. A boy is sweeping the step, and two doors down a woman beats a rug out of an upper window. Nobody is staring at the yard. Everyone is busy with something.

Sefa stays at the gate with her hand on the grey plank. From there she can see the stair, the bright padlock and the low kitchen door, and anyone who comes out of it will see her first.

From where he stands, the open half of the gate frames a strip of the Coast Way, and he studies that strip the way he was taught to on the Wide.

A cart rolls past and blocks the view for a moment. When it has gone the street looks just as it did. Whoever chalked that post either knows his trade as well as Pell does or has moved off. From the back of the yard Pell can't tell which.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps in from the gate, unhurried, and stops a few paces from the foot of the stair with her hands plainly open. "Mistress Pike. You have a right to the money and a right to be careful. Three and four is a plain sum." She lets one hand rest at her purse, but doesn't open it. "Before any box goes down those stairs, I'd like to see the room and the account, with you at the door. If the seal's whole and all's as your lodger left it, the debt can be settled out of our own purses—you'll lose nothing."

Her voice softens. "The other one who came asking. What did he look like, and did he offer to settle with you, or just to carry the box off?" She watches Wenna's hands rather than her face as she asks.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell comes back up the yard at an easy walk, hands where she can see them, and stops a little short of the stair so he's not crowding her — but close enough to read her hands when she answers.

"Fair's fair, Mistress Pike. A room's a room and a dead man's rent doesn't pay itself." He glances at Bram. "Three and four. We can settle that out of the fee and take it off the top before Vell counts his shares — he'd rather pay rent than argue with a landlady, and if he'd rather argue, that's his quarrel with her, not ours." He's already fishing the purse out, slow, letting the coin be seen. "I'll put it in your hand myself if it saves a walk."

Then, lighter, as if it's an afterthought: "You said *him*. Who came asking before us? Broad fellow, quiet, talks like the Gate? And what did he offer — the rent, or more than the rent?" He nods up at the gallery without looking away from her. "And that padlock's new since the brother went home. Yours? Or did somebody put it on and give you the key?"

He keeps the purse open but not yet paying — the coin is for after she's answered.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I fold Odda’s letter and tuck it deep inside my coat. For a moment I stand still, jaw tight, then turn back to Wenna.

“Not Vell’s men beyond this errand. And you shouldn’t lose your rent over it.” I count out three gold and four silver from my own purse. “A receipt, please, so I can put the expense to him.”

I bring out Vell’s order for her to inspect.

“Who came before us, and what did he want? We can talk up on the gallery, out of Tobin’s way. No need to unlock anything just yet.”

I gesture for Sefa to join us, leaving room for her beside Wenna.

scenes.narration:
Sefa comes in from the gate with her hands open and stops a few paces short of the stair. Wenna lets her finish. She looks at the open hands, then at the purse Sefa hasn't touched, and says nothing yet. Pell comes up the yard from the staves at the same easy walk and stops just outside arm's reach. He has his purse out and open, so the coin shows. Wenna's eyes go to it and stay there a moment.

Bram doesn't wait for her answer. He stands still a moment with his jaw set, then counts three gold and four silver out of his own purse into his palm and holds it out to her. He gives her Vell's folded order with the other hand.

She takes the coin first. She weighs it in her hand, counts it with her thumb, and only then takes the paper. She looks at the red wax and the key between the letters, and hands the order back to him unopened.

"That's it paid." She drops the coins into her apron pocket and turns to Pell. "Put that away. I don't get paid twice for one room." She goes back into the kitchen. When she comes out she has a little rent book with a greasy cover and a stub of pencil. She writes slowly, licking the pencil, tears the leaf out and gives it to Bram: *Recd of Bram Halloway three gold four silver rent owing Jassan Ferr middle room paid in full. W. Pike.* The letters are big and careful, the hand of someone who learned to write late.

Bram nods at the gallery, and she goes up ahead of them with one hand on the rail. The stair creaks under Bram's chain mail. At the top she stops by the middle door with her back to it, the key on its cord in her fist. Now that she's been paid, the answers come.

"Big through the shoulders. Quiet. Talks like the Gate." She gives Pell a short look. "Like you. Said Thale sent him. He came round the day after they carried Jassan down, and again yesterday. The rent, and two gold over for my trouble, and he takes the lot. Box, books, bedding, all of it." She folds her arms. "I didn't say yes. Vell's a moneylender. I wasn't having him on my step saying I'd sold his box out from under him. He said he'd come back this afternoon and ask me again."

The padlock is hers. "Mine. Got it off Garth at the chandler's the same morning. A dead man's door, people start getting ideas." Nobody has been in since the bearers took Jassan down, she says, only her. "Once. To strip the bed and open the window for the smell. Then I shut it again." When she says *once*, her hands stop on the apron and stay there, flat, the way they didn't for anything else. Pell has watched people hold things back for a living, and Sefa has watched them do it at sickbeds. Both of them see it: she has told them the truth and left a piece out. Neither of them can tell which piece.

From the gallery you can see straight across the lane, over the chandler's awning. The boy is still sweeping. Nobody is leaning on the awning post now. Up the Coast Way toward the town an apple core lies in the gutter, and beyond it a pair of broad shoulders is walking away, no faster than anyone else in the street, until a cart turns in between and hides them.

Wenna turns her back on the street and puts the key into the bright padlock. She doesn't turn it.

"Paid's paid. Room's yours to clear by sundown. I open it when you say, and I stand right here while you're in."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slides the purse back into his coat without a word about it. She's right; a landlady who won't be paid twice is a landlady he'd trust further than most.

"Open it, Mistress Pike. Then let me go in first and alone for the length of a breath or two before the chain mail follows — not because I doubt you, but because a floor tells you things before it's been walked on." He says it mild, a craftsman asking for room at the bench. "Bram, Sefa — stay on the gallery with her a moment. And one of you keep an eye down the Way. Our broad friend was on the awning post when we came in and he's walking off toward town now, no faster than anyone else. That's a man going to tell somebody we're here, not a man giving up. He said this afternoon. I'd believe him."

He waits for the padlock to come off, then before he steps over the threshold he crouches at the door and looks: the sill, the dust on the boards, whether the window shutter's latch sits as she left it, the bed stripped as she said, and — most of all — whether there's a forearm's length of oak with iron corners anywhere in sight, and whether the wax on it is red, whole, and pressed only once.

Over his shoulder, quietly, to Wenna, not accusing, almost kind: "You went in once. Stripped the bed, opened the window. Was there anything else in the room that morning that isn't in it now? A paper, a purse, a letter with a name on it? I'm not Vell and I'm not the Fist. I'd just rather hear it from you up here than find out from Thale's man this afternoon."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I tuck the receipt beside Vell’s order and shift aside so I’m not crowding Wenna against the door.

“Before we open it—when you went in to strip the bed, did you find anything, or move anything besides the bedding? Even something small. Better we hear it from you than guess wrong.”

I keep my voice quiet, without accusation. While she answers, I glance to Pell for his readiness.

Once he’s ready, I nod to Wenna. “Go ahead. We’ll look before we touch.”

I stay by the doorway, leaving Pell room to inspect it and keeping the stairs in view.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa glances once toward the gutter and the broad back walking away, then looks at the padlock and the shut middle door. "We're not in a hurry to put hands on anything before we've looked," she says quietly. "Only—"

She catches Pell's eye and tips her head toward the chandler's awning, then back toward the door. "Someone was leaning there when we arrived, eating an apple. Now he's walking toward town, taking his time. Big through the shoulders. So before that lock turns, I want the door watched and the gallery clear behind us. And I want to be the first to listen at it. A room shut three days." She does not say *a dead man's room*, but it's in the way she stills. "If something's breathing on the other side, I'd rather hear it than meet it."

Pell puts the purse back inside his coat. Wenna watches it go and says nothing more about it. Bram tucks the receipt in beside Vell's order and steps sideways along the rail so she isn't pinned against the door. He asks his question quietly: did she find anything, or move anything, besides the bedding?

Pell's question comes over his shoulder almost at the same moment, low and nearly kind. Wenna looks from one of them to the other.

"Bedding off. Window open, then shut again. I swept round the bed." She jerks her chin at the door. "His papers and that box I never touched. What a clerk writes down is no business of mine." Pell asks whether anything was in the room that morning that isn't in it now. She gives him a longer look than she gave Bram. "Nothing that wasn't owed me." She says nothing after it.

Sefa steps up before the key turns. Wenna moves aside half a pace, frowning, and lets her put her ear to the planks. The wood is warm from the sun on the gallery. Behind it there is nothing alive. A fly ticks against the inside of the shutter, stops, then ticks again. Down in the yard Tobin's hammer keeps its slow time, and that's all. Nothing breathes on the other side and nothing shifts its weight. It is just a room that has been shut up in the heat.

Across the lane the boy has finished sweeping and gone inside. The awning post has nobody leaning on it. Up the Coast Way the carts come and go, and the broad shoulders don't come back.

Bram nods. Wenna turns the key, lifts the bright padlock off the hasp and pushes the door inward with two fingers. "A breath or two. I'm at this door." She stays planted on the sill.

The smell comes out first. It's stale and close, with old tallow in it and something bitter under that. Pell crouches on the threshold before he puts a foot inside.

The room is small. There's a bed with its bare straw mattress, a table under the back window with a stool pushed in, and a nightstand. A cold grate is cut into the side wall. By the door there are two pegs, a hat hanging on one and nothing on the other. The light from the doorway reaches about halfway across, and the shutter keeps the rest dim.

The floor tells Pell less than he hoped. Three days of dust lie thin and even along the walls, and one set of tracks crosses it: a woman's narrow shoes, from the door to the bed, from the bed to the window and back. Around the bed the dust doesn't lie at all. Wenna's broom has been there, in long flat strokes that took everything with them. Whatever the floor near the bed had to say, she swept it up on her one visit. Pell looks across the boards twice and finds nothing in them except her broom.

What he can see doesn't need the floor. On the table under the window, square to its edge the way a clerk would leave it, stands a box a forearm long. It's oak, with iron at the corners, two drop handles and a brass plate on the lid. Wax runs over the hasp in a fat, whole bead, and it isn't red. Even in the dim light it's dark green, like ivy, and the mark pressed into it is round. Vell's ring is square.

On the nightstand by the bed stands a small dark vial with its stopper in. Beside it on the boards is a stain the size of a palm, dried brown and soaked into the grain. The bitter smell is strongest there. In the grate a twist of paper lies on the ash, curled and black at one end, with brown, unburnt paper at the other.

Behind Pell, Wenna stays on the sill with her arms folded, her eyes on the box and nowhere else.

 Pell gives the floor a second, slower look from the threshold, board by board along the walls and in under the bed frame. This time he looks for anything out of true: a nail head brighter than the rest, a seam wider than its neighbours, a board that sits a hair proud. He doesn't find one. Both looks come up empty. From the doorway he can't tell whether anything under those boards has been moved or hidden. Wenna's broom has left them flat, swept and quiet, and the only story the floor tells him is hers.

The fly goes on ticking against the inside of the shutter. Down in the yard Tobin's hammer comes down again.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I remain on the gallery, watching the stairs and gate while Pell examines the room.

“There’s a bitter smell under the tallow, Sefa. Might be worth finding its source before we carry anything out.”

Then, quietly to Wenna: “You said nothing that wasn’t owed you. What did you take against the debt? I’ve just paid the rent in full, so let’s have the account straight.”

I keep my tone matter-of-fact and my hands away from my weapons.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays a step back while Pell reads the floor, one hand on the jamb. The stale, waxy air makes her breathe through her mouth.

"Mistress Pike." Her voice is low, pitched for the doorway rather than the yard. "The strongbox on the table under the back window—is that where it stood all along, and is the table's place the same?" She keeps her eyes on the room, but lets Wenna answer from the sill.

Then she murmurs to Pell, "If the floor's yours, I'll light the corners before either of us crosses." She doesn't wait for an answer; she takes a copper coin from her pouch, holds it in her palm, and a small, steady light kindles in the coin as if a flame had been cupped inside it. She does not enter yet, just lets the light lean past her into the room, away from the bright morning behind them.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't step in yet. He stays crouched on the sill a heartbeat longer, then speaks without turning, low enough that it's for the gallery and not the yard.

"Box is here. On the table, square to the edge, like he left it to go to bed." A pause. "Wax on the hasp is whole. And it's green. Round seal. Vell's is red and square." He lets that land. "So either Vell sealed it with a ring he didn't show us, or somebody else sealed Jassan Ferr's box before Jassan Ferr stopped breathing — and whoever it was, it wasn't done in a hurry. That's a fat, careful bead."

Then he stands and goes in — along the wall where the dust is already disturbed by Wenna's shoes, not across the swept middle — and goes first not to the box but to the nightstand. He doesn't touch the vial. He bends and smells it, and the stain, and looks at the stopper: wax, cork, whether it's been drawn and put back. "Mistress Pike. This vial. Was it here the morning you found him? And the stain — was that wet?" He keeps his voice level. "The brother said heart. Did the brother see this?"

He crosses to the grate, crouches, and with the tip of a dagger — not his fingers — eases the twist of paper off the ash onto the hearthstone so the unburnt end can be read without crumbling the black end. "Sefa, you read a clerk's hand better than I do. Come in along the wall, where her tracks are. Don't cross the middle yet. There's a half-burnt paper here I'd like two pairs of eyes on." Then to Bram, still at the door: "Keep the stair. If our broad friend's gone to fetch coin or company, we've got less of the morning than we thought. And Bram — nobody touches that wax. Not us, not her, not Vell till he's standing over it saying out loud it isn't his."

Last, he glances at the back shutter's latch from where he kneels — checking it's seated the way a woman would leave it after closing a window for the smell, and not the way a man would leave it after coming in by the lean-to roof.

His tone is matter-of-fact and his hands are kept away from his weapons.

She asks Wenna, in a voice pitched for the doorway, whether the strongbox under the back window and the table have always stood where they do. She tells you that if the floor is yours, she'll light the corners before either of you crosses. Wenna answers without turning her head. The box is where he kept it, on the table under the window, and she never shifted either. She watches the box as she speaks, and watches the glowing coin a moment longer.

The light is small and steady, and the shadows behind the shutter pull back. The far corners are only corners: dust, a cobweb hanging from the grate's lintel, a dropped quill-feather under the table legs. The green bead on the hasp catches the light. Pell crouches at the grate with his dagger and starts working the tip under the paper's brown end to lift it off the ash.

Pell gets the dagger tip under the brown end and lifts. The paper comes up with it. The black end doesn't. It folds in on itself as it leaves the ash, then breaks off and falls apart into grey flakes on the hearthstone. When he lays the scrap down, it is half the size it was, a curl of brown paper with a scorched edge. A clerk's hand runs across it, small and even, the same hand line after line.

The top line has survived whole: *To Sergeant Cowl of the Fist,*. Below it most of a line has gone with the ash. Under that is the last thing left before the scorch: *the notes were sold before*. Whatever came after those words is in the flakes at his knee now.

From where he kneels he can see the back shutter. The latch hook sits down in its eye, square and neat, the way it falls when someone pulls a shutter to from inside and drops the hook without forcing it.

Out on the gallery, Bram puts his question to Wenna quietly. He paid the room in full, so what did she take against the debt?

She doesn't answer straight away. She dries her hands on her apron, though they're dry already. Her eyes go to the two pegs by the door, the hat on one and nothing on the other, and come back to Bram.

"You paid the room." Her voice is flat, but not hard. "I said I don't get paid twice. I don't." She reaches into her apron pocket, picks out one of the gold coins he gave her and puts it back in his palm. "There. That's square. What it was is my business, and it's gone, and it was owed." She folds her arms again and looks out at the lane rather than at him.

The coin is still warm from her pocket. Down in the yard, Tobin's hammer comes down on the hoop. Across the lane the boy has come back out with a pail and is sluicing the chandler's step, and the Coast Way is all carts and dust in the sun. Nobody is leaning on anything.

<<<
Bram Halloway: I remain on the gallery, watching the stairs and gate while Pell examines the room.

“There’s a bitter smell under the tallow, Sefa. Might be worth finding its source before we carry anything out.”

Then, quietly to Wenna: “You said nothing that wasn’t owed you. What did you take against the debt? I’ve just paid the rent in full, so let’s have the account straight.”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa stays a step back while Pell reads the floor, one hand on the jamb. The stale, waxy air makes her breathe through her mouth.

Then she murmurs to Pell, "If the floor's yours, I'll light the corners before either of us crosses." She doesn't wait for an answer; she takes a copper coin from her pouch, holds it in her palm, and a small, steady light kindles in the coin as if a flame had been cupped inside it. She does not enter yet, just lets the light lean past her into the room, away from the bright morning behind them.

Pell Dunmore: Pell doesn't step in yet. He stays crouched on the sill a heartbeat longer, then speaks without turning, low enough that it's for the gallery and not the yard.

"Box is here. On the table, square to the edge, like he left it to go to bed." A pause. "Wax on the hasp is whole. And it's green. Round seal. Vell's is red and square." He lets that land. "So either Vell sealed it with a ring he didn't show us, or somebody else sealed Jassan Ferr's box before Jassan Ferr stopped breathing — and whoever it was, it wasn't done in a hurry. That's a fat, careful bead."

Then he stands and goes in — along the wall where the dust is already disturbed by Wenna's shoes, not across the swept middle — and goes first not to the box but to the nightstand. He doesn't touch the vial. He bends and smells it, and the stain, and looks at the stopper: wax, cork, whether it's been drawn and put back. "Mistress Pike. This vial. Was it here the morning you found him? And the stain — was that wet?" He keeps his voice level. "The brother said heart. Did the brother see this?"

He crosses to the grate, crouches, and with the tip of a dagger — not his fingers — eases the twist of paper off the ash onto the hearthstone so the unburnt end can be read without crumbling the black end. - Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps in along Wenna's tracks, careful not to widen them, her glowing coin held low. The room tightens around the smell—tallow, old sweat, and that green bitterness under it. She stops where Pell crouches at the grate, sinks to her heels, and reads the curl of brown paper by her own light.

*To Sergeant Cowl of the Fist.* Then the scorch, then: *the notes were sold before.*

She turns the words over in her head before she speaks them aloud, softly enough that only Pell hears. "He was going to tell the Fist something about notes being sold. But the letter didn't burn itself." She keeps her eyes on the blackened edge, then glances toward the nightstand. "A man with a weak heart doesn't usually write to a sergeant, then carry his medicine in an unstoppered brown vial that smells like a garden left too long in the sun."

She rises, still not touching anything, and lets the light drift back toward the nightstand. "The vial and the half-sun on the scrap. Pell, if that's alchemy, it's not the kind my sisters kept. Can you tell what it is? What did you make of the box's green seal—it's not the ring he showed us."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell looks at the scrap a long moment. Then he takes the receipt-leaf's twin — a blank page torn from the back of his own little ration tally in the pack — folds the brown curl inside it flat, and tucks it into the inner pocket of his coat where the purse was. He does it slowly, so Wenna on the sill can see what he's taking and that it isn't hers.

"Mistress Pike. This was in his grate. A letter he started and burnt. It's addressed to a sergeant of the Fist. Does the name Cowl mean anything to you? Did Jassan ever have a trooper up here, or go down to the Fist's post in town?"

He stands and comes back along the wall to the doorway, and speaks for the gallery only, flat and quick. "Three things, and none of them are heart. One: the seal on that box is green and round, and Vell told us red and square — so either he lied about his own ring or somebody else had a key to this room and time to melt wax in it. Two: the vial on the stand has a little half-sun inked on the tag. That's Lathander's mark. That's the Song of the Morning's mark. And the brother from the Song picked it up, smelled it, set it down and said *heart*. Three—" he taps his coat where the scrap is, "Jassan Ferr was writing to a Sergeant Cowl of the Fist. All that's left of it says *the notes were sold before*. A clerk's phrase. A moneylender sells a man's debt to one buyer, then sells the same paper to another — and the ledgers in that box are the only place it'd show." He looks at Bram. "That's why the fee's seventy-five and not fifteen. That's why Thale wants it, and that's why Vell talks about the wax like it's his neck."

He breathes out. "I'm a hireling. I take the box to the man who hired me — that's the job and I'll do it. But I'm not carrying it down that stair with a seal on it that isn't his and letting him tell me afterwards I broke it. Sefa — can you make a fair copy of that seal's shape, or press it in a bit of candle-wax from the nightstand so we've a record of it whole before it leaves this room? And I want that vial wrapped and in my satchel, stopper in, tag on. If a brother of the Song called it heart, a *different* brother of the Song can tell us what it actually is, this afternoon, before Thale's man comes back to ask Wenna again."

Then, quieter, to Wenna, not pressing: "The empty peg. Was it a coat? I only ask because if Jassan Ferr went to the Fist's post, he went wearing it, and a sergeant might remember the coat before he remembers the man."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I put the coin away. “Square, then.” I leave the empty peg alone.

Still watching the approach, I ask Wenna, “The brother who came—what was his name? If you didn’t catch it, what did he look like? We may need to ask him about that medicine.”

To Sefa and Pell, quietly: “I’ve the stair. Before we move the box, let’s record that seal exactly. Our order bears Vell’s mark for comparison.”

"You paid the room. I said I don't get paid twice. I don't." She takes one of the gold coins he gave her out of her apron pocket and puts it back in his palm. "There. That's square. What it was is my business, and it's gone, and it was owed." Then she folds her arms and looks out at the lane instead of at him.

That coin is the extra gold in your purse. The coin is still warm from her pocket. Bram can read for himself that she gave back one gold and wouldn't say what for, and that her glance went to the empty peg. She didn't name the thing, and she clearly means to leave it there.

Bram is still at the doorway, where he can see the stair and the gate. Below, Tobin's hammer keeps its slow time. Across the lane the boy has come back out with a pail and is sluicing the chandler's step. The Coast Way is carts and dust, and nobody is leaning on anything.

scenes.narration:
Sefa comes in along Wenna's narrow tracks with the coin held low, and its light goes ahead of her across the boards. She sinks onto her heels beside Pell at the grate. By her own light the clerk's hand is easy to read: *To Sergeant Cowl of the Fist,* then the scorch, then *the notes were sold before*. She says what she makes of it quietly, for Pell. When she stands she doesn't touch anything. She lets the light lean toward the nightstand.

Close up, the vial is as Pell left it. The cork sits snug in the neck, and the dried drip runs down the dark glass to the stain on the boards. The thread holds the little half-sun tag tight round the neck. The bitterness is strongest down here, the smell of green stems left too long in water. The light runs across the bare mattress and the swept boards and the dust under the bed frame. Nothing else in that corner looks different with light on it.

Pell looks at the brown curl a while longer. Then he tears a blank leaf from the back of his ration tally, slides the scrap onto it with the dagger's flat, folds it over and puts it in the inner pocket of his coat. He does it slowly, facing the door. Wenna watches his hands do it and lets it go.

"Cowl." She says it the way people say the name of a man everyone in town knows. "Sergeant at the Fist post by the market. Red in the face, loud. No trooper ever came up my stair. Where Jassan went when he wasn't at Vell's I couldn't say." She looks at the cold grate. "He wrote of an evening. Candle went late most nights. That's all I know about his letters."

Pell comes back along the wall to the doorway and lays out his three points for the gallery, low and quick: the wrong wax, the half-sun, the sergeant. When he gets to *somebody else had a key to this room*, Wenna's head comes round.

"Nobody had my key." She says it flat and hard. "It's on my cord or it's on my hip. That box was sealed the way you see it before he ever went to bed that night, or I'd have smelled the wax." Then, short, to Pell's wish about the vial: "Take the bottle if you want it. I don't want it in my house."

He asks about the empty peg. She looks at it, not at him.

"It was a coat. Grey wool, good." Her hand moves to her apron and stops. "It's gone. Ask your sergeant about the man. The coat won't be coming back up my stair."

Sefa Marrin: Sefa steps in along Wenna's tracks, careful not to widen them, her glowing coin held low. The room tightens around the smell—tallow, old sweat, and that green bitterness under it. She stops where Pell crouches at the grate, sinks to her heels, and reads the curl of brown paper by her own light.

*To Sergeant Cowl of the Fist.* Then the scorch, then: *the notes were sold before.*

She turns the words over in her head before she speaks them aloud, softly enough that only Pell hears. "He was going to tell the Fist something about notes being sold. But the letter didn't burn itself." She keeps her eyes on the blackened edge, then glances toward the nightstand. "A man with a weak heart doesn't usually write to a sergeant, then carry his medicine in an unstoppered brown vial that smells like a garden left too long in the sun."

She rises, still not touching anything, and lets the light drift back toward the nightstand. "The vial and the half-sun on the scrap. Pell, if that's alchemy, it's not the kind my sisters kept. Can you tell what it is? What did you make of the box's green seal—it's not the ring he showed us."

Pell Dunmore: Pell looks at the scrap a long moment. Then he takes the receipt-leaf's twin — a blank page torn from the back of his own little ration tally in the pack — folds the brown curl inside it flat, and tucks it into the inner pocket of his coat where the purse was. He does it slowly, so Wenna on the sill can see what he's taking and that it isn't hers.

"Mistress Pike. This was in his grate. A letter he started and burnt. It's addressed to a sergeant of the Fist. Does the name Cowl mean anything to you? Did Jassan ever have a trooper up here, or go down to the Fist's post in town?"

He stands and comes back along the wall to the doorway, and speaks for the gallery only, flat and quick. "Three things, and none of them are heart. One: the seal on that box is green and round, and Vell told us red and square — so either he lied about his own ring or somebody else had a key to this room and time to melt wax in it. Two: the vial on the stand has a little half-sun inked on the tag. That's Lathander's mark. That's the Song of the Morning's mark. And the brother from the Song picked it up, smelled it, set it down and said *heart*. Three—" he taps his coat where the scrap is, "Jassan Ferr was writing to a Sergeant Cowl of the Fist. All that's left of it says *the notes were sold before*. A clerk's phrase. A moneylender sells a man's debt to one buyer, then sells the same paper to another — and the ledgers in that box are the only place it'd show." He looks at Bram. "That's why the fee's seventy-five and not fifteen. That's why Thale wants it, and that's why Vell talks about the wax like it's his neck."

He breathes out. "I'm a hireling. I take the box to the man who hired me — that's the job and I'll do it. But I'm not carrying it down that stair with a seal on it that isn't his and letting him tell me afterwards I broke it. Sefa — can you make a fair copy of that seal's shape, or press it in a bit of candle-wax from the nightstand so we've a record of it whole before it leaves this room? And I want that vial wrapped and in my satchel, stopper in, tag on. If a brother of the Song called it heart, a *different* brother of the Song can tell us what it actually is, this afternoon, before Thale's man comes back to ask Wenna again."

Then, quieter, to Wenna, not pressing: "The empty peg. Was it a coat? I only ask because if Jassan Ferr went to the Fist's post, he went wearing it, and a sergeant might remember the coat before he remembers the man."

Bram Halloway: I put the coin away. “Square, then.” I leave the empty peg alone.

Still watching the approach, I ask Wenna, “The brother who came—what was his name? If you didn’t catch it, what did he look like? We may need to ask him about that medicine.”

To Sefa and Pell, quietly: “I’ve the stair. Before we move the box, let’s record that seal exactly. Our order bears Vell’s mark for comparison.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell nods at Wenna — *the coat, owed, fine* — and leaves it there. A landlady who gives back a gold piece she could have kept has told him all he needs about what she took and why.

He kneels at the grate again and picks up a stick of cold charcoal, the black end of a burnt splint. "Sefa, give me your light on the hasp a moment." He tears a second blank leaf from his ration tally, lays it flat over the green bead, and rubs the charcoal across it light and even, the way a boy takes a brass off a tomb — the round mark, its device, the edge of the bead, the join where wax meets iron. He lifts it off without the paper touching anything but wax, checks it against the light, and holds it so Bram can set Vell's red square beside it. "There. Round. Not his. Dated by the bell, witnessed by three and Wenna Pike's own eyes. If Vell says we broke it, that's what I lay on his counter." He folds it in with the letter.

Then the vial: he takes the cloth that wraps his rations, winds it round the dark glass with the tag still on and the cork still in, and settles it upright in the healer's satchel between two potions where it won't roll. "That's ours. Not Vell's."

Only now does he go to the table and put both hands on the drop handles. He lifts the box an inch, feels the weight shift, tilts it a hair and listens — whether something slides inside like bound books, or whether it's lighter than seventy-five gold has any right to be. He sets it down again. "Right. It goes down the stair with me carrying and Bram's shield in front. Nobody sets it on the ground between here and the counting-house." He looks at the other two. "But the Song's on the way up the hill, more or less, and the bell says we've the whole of the day. I'd like Sefa to put her head in and ask for Brother Aldane — a novice of the hospice asking a brother about a sick man's medicine is the most natural thing in Faerûn. Ten minutes. I'll stand in the porch with the box in my arms and Bram at my shoulder, and if the old man says *heart* twice, I'll want to see his face when he says it."

He turns to Wenna last, civil. "Thale's man comes back this afternoon. When he does, tell him the truth — Vell's hirelings took it on Vell's paper, and you've the receipt. Don't tell him which way we went." He pauses on the sill. "And Mistress Pike — if a red-faced sergeant ever does come up your stair asking after Jassan Ferr's letters, there's one he didn't finish. I've got it. He can find me through Vell's counter, or he can find me not at all."

He hefts the box and waits for Bram to take the stair first.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I turn toward the room without pointing down the lane.

“Two idle men at the townward corner. Could be nothing, but assume we’ll be followed. Copy the seal by drawing, not pressing—we don’t risk cracking it.”

I draw Sefa and Pell close enough to speak without carrying to the yard.

“There’s something else you should know. A runner brought me a letter. Odda Brand says her house stands against forty gold Harl owed Vell. Says Jassan warned her the debt would be called once this box returns. She asks me to buy the note before he opens it.”

I let them read the letter, keeping it out of Wenna’s hands.

“If those debts were sold already, that matters to her. But we’ve suspicions, not proof. I won’t open the box behind your backs.”

I look to Pell. “Did you find a usable way out at the back?”

Then to Wenna: “Who bought the coat? You mentioned the sergeant—was it him? We’re not asking you to fetch it back.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps closer to the table, outside the dust of Wenna's swept path, and lowers the glowing coin until the green wax comes fully into the light. She doesn't touch the box; she lets the little flame circle it just above the hasp, as if drawing it in the air.

"Then let's not argue over who sealed it," she says quietly. "Let's look at it while there's still morning light." She raises her free hand and moves her fingers through a small, precise shape. A faint image appears in the air just to the side of the hasp—an exact likeness of the green wax bead as the light catches it, the same colour, the same thickness, the same roundness. She sharpens it with a breath of concentration: a perfect copy, nothing more, hovering where both she and Pell can study it without once touching the real thing.

"The seal's impression," she murmurs. "Not impression enough, but the form and colour, against Vell's red square ring. We can take the likeness in our heads if we can't take the wax." She looks toward Wenna in the doorway, her voice still gentle. "Mistress Pike, was the vial the only bottle or packet of his you ever saw? Did he take powders, teas, anything from the Song besides that?"

scenes.narration:
Sefa's coin is already moving. She brings it down toward the table, and the little light slides across the oak and pools on the hasp just as Pell asks for it. He kneels at the grate and picks a cold, black splint end out of the ash. Then he tears a second blank leaf from his ration tally, crosses the room inside Wenna's tracks and lays the paper over the green bead, lightly, the way you'd lay a cloth over a sleeping face. The room is warm with sun on the shutter. The wax under the paper is warm too.

Pell does it in short, even strokes and keeps his wrist off the paper, so all the weight is in the charcoal and none of it in his hand. The paper takes the dome of the bead, then the rim, then the device pressed into the middle. When he peels the leaf back, the green bead on the hasp is exactly as it was, fat and whole and pressed once. On the paper, in grey and black, is a round mark the size of a thumbnail: a pair of balanced scales, and under them an eye drawn shut, a single curved line with lashes. At the edge of the rubbing the charcoal has caught something else too, a thin hard ring where the wax stops. Up close in Sefa's light you can see what it is. The green wax isn't sitting on the iron. It's laid over a disc of dull grey lead that has been pinched around the hasp, the way old bonds were sealed when people wanted the seal to outlast the paper.

Bram speaks low from the doorway, *by drawing, not pressing*, as Pell lifts the leaf clear. Pell holds it up beside the order. Vell's red square, with its key between O and V, looks nothing like the scales and the shut eye. Pell folds the rubbing in with the burnt letter.

He winds the dark vial in his ration cloth with the cork still in and the tag still on, and stands it upright in the healer's satchel between two red flasks. Wenna watches it go into the bag. Her shoulders come down a little.

Then he puts both hands on the drop handles and lifts. The box is honestly heavy, about what a full bucket of water weighs, and when he tilts it a hair the weight inside slides. It's the soft, blunt shove of bound books shifting against each other, and then they settle. Nothing rattles and nothing chinks. It's paper, and plenty of it.

Bram draws the other two in close by the table, where the hammering in the yard covers voices, and tells them about the two idle men at the corner and about the letter. He takes it out of his coat and holds it so Sefa and Pell can read it and Wenna, on the sill, can't:

*Bram — Harl died owing Ostrin Vell forty gold. Vell's note for it is in his dead clerk's strongbox with the rest; Jassan wrote to me before he died that it will be called on the house the day after the box goes back. Vell's counting-house sells such a note back for its face to whoever pays it at the counter before it is entered in his books. If you can, pay the forty gold for it before nightfall, before the box is opened, and the house stays ours. I have nothing left to give. — Odda Brand*

The hand is unsteady, and the ink went blotchy where the pen was pressed too hard. Whatever Wenna catches of the murmur behind her, it isn't enough. She has turned half toward the gallery rail with her eyes on the lane.

Sefa lowers the coin until its light lies right on the hasp and slowly circles the green bead with it, a finger's width above the wax. In that light the wax isn't plain. Down inside it, under the surface, there's a fine grain, close whorls and ridges like the pad of a thumb, except no thumb ever had lines like these. They don't sit still. When the light moves they seem to turn to keep facing it.

Her palms go warm, both of them, the one holding the coin and the empty one, as if she had cupped them round a lamp chimney. The light in the coin leans toward the wax on its own, the way a flame leans into a draught. It is pointing at what lies under the seal and at what lies beyond the box. Close by, in a voice like a wick catching, the Lantern speaks once:

*Only a little more owed.*

Then there is only the warmth, and the coin's light leaning, waiting for her.

Her other hand moves through its small, precise shape, and a second bead hangs in the air beside the hasp. It has the same ivy-dark green, the same fat roundness, the same scales and the same shut eye, true to the last lash. Side by side the difference is plain. The copy is colour and shape and nothing else. Its wax is flat all the way through. The grain inside the real bead doesn't come across into the likeness, and no care she takes with the image puts it there.

Wenna answers Sefa's question first, and she answers it easily. "That bottle. Since about midwinter. Drops in his water of a night, I'd hear the spoon on the cup. Nothing else, no powders, no teas. He wasn't one for physic." She dries her hands on her apron. "He'd go up the hill for it himself."

To Bram she gives a short shake of the head. "Cowl's never been on my stair. I told you." Then, flatter: "The coat went where a coat was wanted. It's gone, I'm square, and that's the end of it." She folds her arms and won't say any more about the coat.

Pell's word about Thale's man she takes without arguing. "He'll hear what's so. Vell's paper, Vell's people, receipt in my book." Her mouth twists. "Which way you went, I'm in my kitchen. I don't see the lane from my kitchen." And when he mentions the letter for the sergeant, she just says, "He'd have to climb my stair first," and steps back off the sill onto the gallery to make room for the box.

Pell stands in the doorway with the box in both arms, square against his chest, waiting.

Out on the gallery the sun has moved off the rail. Up at the smithy corner the man on the mounting block has got to his feet and is stretching his back. The one by the wall hasn't moved. Neither of them is looking at the yard, carefully. Down below, Tobin knocks a finished barrel onto its side and rolls it to the gate.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I tuck Odda’s letter away once the others have had a chance to read it, then return to the doorway to keep the stairs and the two men at the corner in view.

“Whoever carries the box will need both hands. I’ll keep mine free and walk on the exposed side.”

For now I leave the strongbox untouched, waiting for Pell’s word on the back way and Wenna’s answer about the coat.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds the little green copy in the air a moment longer, studying it against the real wax, then lets it fade rather than leave a false seal floating over a dead man's strongbox.

She turns her head toward Pell and Bram. "What have you turned up while I was staring at this wax? Show me flat and in my light, not in the doorway. And Mistress Pike—if you know anything more, I'd hear it now." She steps around to the table but keeps her hands well off it, eyes searching what the men have found.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stands in the doorway with the weight of it against his chest and looks at the rubbing once more before he folds it away for good.

"Scales and a shut eye, on lead under the wax. That's a bond seal, the kind a notary puts on a thing he wants to outlast the paper inside it — and scales with a blind eye is the Blind God's mark. Tyr's house, or someone borrowing it." He says it slow. "Jassan Ferr didn't lock up his master's books. He had them *witnessed*. He made evidence, and then he wrote to the Fist, and then his heart stopped. And now the man whose books they are wants them back with the seal he *didn't* put on them still whole, so he can say nobody read them." A short breath. "I've carried worse for worse men. But I'll say it once so it's said: I don't like this box."

He turns to Bram, low. "The back's a lean-to roof and a nettle lane with a ditch. Good for me alone with empty hands. No good for chain mail, and no good for this — I'm not dropping seventy-five gold of somebody's ruin into a ditch. We go out the front, all three, box in the middle, straight up the smith street in the sun. Nobody robs three armed people between a Fist trooper and forty hammers at midmorning. The two at the corner want to see which way we turn, not to take it. Let them see."

"But Vell said *before nightfall*, not *before noon*. So here's the day." He nods up the hill. "The Song first. A temple's a safe place to set a box down — nobody's robbing Lathander's porch — and Sefa asks for Brother Aldane and what a half-sun vial of green bitter is for. While she does, Bram, you go to Vell's counter without us and without the box, and you buy Odda Brand's note *now*, while he still needs you. He'll sell it cheap to a man who's holding his box. Don't tell him where it is. Tell him it's safe and coming at dusk, and that his wax is whole." A thin smile. "Which is true. It's just not his wax."

"And the letter to Cowl?" He pats his coat. "That doesn't go to Vell. Ever. We decide between us by dusk whether it goes to the sergeant. Agreed? Then Bram takes the stair first."

scenes.narration:
Bram folds Odda's letter along its old creases and puts it back inside his coat, behind Vell's order and the receipt. He goes back to the doorway, where he can see the stair, the gate and the corner. He says the carrier will need both hands, so his own stay empty and he walks on the open side. He doesn't go near the box.

Sefa lets the green copy go. It doesn't fall. It just thins until the dust behind it shows through, and then there's nothing over the table at all. The coin in her palm still glows, and its light still leans the same way, toward the doorway now, where the real bead sits in Pell's arms. The warmth in her hands hasn't gone either. She steps round to the table, keeping her hands off it.

The table has nothing left on it. In the dust where the box stood is a clean oblong, square to the edge, its corners sharp. A box that had been lifted and put back would have left two outlines, or a smeared one. This one is single and true. At the far end of the table a stoppered inkpot and a wiped pen are laid side by side, as neat as the desk at Vell's. Under the table the dropped quill-feather is still lying there.

Pell talks from the doorway with the box against his chest, slowly, and the room hears all of it: the bond seal, the Blind God's mark, the letter to the Fist, the front way out in the sun, the Song first, Bram at Vell's counter alone, the letter to Cowl never going to Vell. Sefa went through temple training, and she was taught Tyr's mark young. The god's scales rest on a warhammer. There's no hammer on the rubbing in Pell's pocket, and none on the wax.

Wenna answers Sefa from the gallery without turning her head.

"More." She thinks about it, and her mouth works. "He went up the hill the day before. Came back with nothing in his hands. Every other time he came back with that bottle." She jerks her chin at Pell's satchel. "He sat up with the candle. Late. I heard the grate going near midnight, and I thought, it's not cold enough for a fire." She stops. "That's all I've got, and I'm not paid for that either."

Down in the yard, someone comes in at the gate.

It's a boy of about ten, barefoot, breathing hard as though he'd run the whole Coast Way. He has a smudge of soot on one cheek. He stops short of Tobin's barrel and doesn't wait for the hammer.

"Big man. Chain coat, shield. Bram." He says the name the way he's been told to, loudly. Tobin points up with the driver without a word, and the boy tips his head back, finds Bram in the doorway and shouts the rest straight up the stair, so the whole yard hears it and the gallery too.

"Mistress Brand says have you been to Vell's counter yet. About the forty. She says she'll be at the almshouse door at the Song till the noon bell, and she'd sooner say the rest to your face." He sucks in a breath. "She says Jassan told her not to wait till it's opened. That's all. She hasn't got a copper for me neither."

Wenna's head comes round at *forty* and *Vell's counter*. She looks at Bram for a long moment and folds her arms over her apron. She says nothing. Tobin's hammer comes down once and stops, and he stands there with the driver resting on the rim.

The boy stays where he is at the foot of the stair, plainly waiting to see if there's an answer to carry back.

Across the lane, at the corner where the Coast Way meets the smithy street, the man by the wall has pushed himself upright. From there the gallery is in plain view: the open middle door, and a thin man standing in it with an oak box held square against his chest. The man looks at it for no longer than you'd look at the weather. Then he turns and walks up the smithy street toward the town, not hurrying. The one on the mounting block sits back down.

Pell stands on the sill with the weight of the box in his arms. The light in Sefa's coin is still leaning toward it.

 (Out of game: none of these four needed a roll. They're positioning, holding back, a cantrip ending and Pell saying his own read aloud. All four happened as declared and are in the narration above. Wenna had already turned down the question about the coat the round before.)

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the coin's light fall across Pell and the oak box, and keeps her voice low. "Before we move that another step, the seal is not Tyr's. His mark is scales over a warhammer. This has the scales and a blind eye, but no hammer. Either someone borrowed the god's look, or they stamped it not knowing the difference. That's worth saying aloud now, while Wenna can still swear no one's tampered with it."

She crosses to the gallery rail without hurrying, looking down at the boy rather than out at the street. "Tell your mistress Bram has heard her message, and he'll come before the noon bell if the road stays clear. Tell her not to wait past it, and don't stop to talk to anyone else along the way."

Then, more quietly, to Bram as he moves to the stair: "Go by the busiest lane. If you glance back, do it for traffic, not for pursuers." She turns her head toward Wenna. "Those two out there—one by the wall, one on the mounting block. Have they been round your gate before, or only since the broad man came asking?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't move off the sill, but his voice comes down the stair before Bram's can, easy and loud enough for the yard — the voice of a hireling with nothing on his mind.

"Boy. The big man's heard you. Tell Mistress Brand *yes, before noon, at the Song.* Nothing else — not the counting-house, not a number. You've said forty once in a cooper's yard already and that's once too often." He shifts the box onto one hip just long enough to fish a copper out and flip it down the stair to him. "That's for the running. Go the long way round the smith street. There's a man walking up it ahead of you and I'd rather he didn't hear what you're carrying."

Then, low, to the other two on the gallery, his back to the lane: "Change of plan, and a small one. That boy just told half the Coast Way that Bram's got business at Vell's counter about forty gold, and the one by the wall took a good look at this box and walked off toward town the moment he heard it. So Bram doesn't go to Vell's alone — not now, not with Thale's man knowing his name and his errand. We all go up to the Song. Odda's at the almshouse door till the noon bell; Bram talks to her there with his own ears, Sefa asks for Brother Aldane, and I sit in the porch with Lathander's doorkeeper and this on my knees. Vell gets his box at dusk like he said. He doesn't get it a minute sooner."

He glances at Sefa. "And you're right about the hammer. I jumped. Scales with no hammer and a shut eye — that's not Tyr's house, that's somebody who wanted it to *look* like a court's seal to anyone who didn't grow up next to a temple. Which means Jassan didn't go to a notary. He went to somebody private. The old brother might know who stamps lead in this town."

Last, to Wenna, as he steps onto the gallery and makes room for Bram to take the stair: "One outline in the dust, Mistress Pike. He set it down once and never lifted it again. You told it true." A nod. "If anyone with Gate shoulders asks, we went up the hill. Everyone goes up the hill."

He waits for Bram's shield to be one step below him, then follows, the box held square and both hands on the handles, Sefa behind with her light put away.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Song first, together,” I tell Pell and Sefa quietly. “Odda’s there, and I need to hear the rest before buying anything. I’ve twenty-two gold all told, not forty. And I won’t tell Vell his wax is whole when we know it isn’t his.”

I check that my sword is loose in its scabbard, shield ready, then take the stairs ahead of Pell, watching the gate.

At the bottom I give the boy two copper. “Thank you. Tell Mistress Brand I haven’t paid yet. We’re coming to the Song now. Don’t tell anyone else our business if they ask.”

I wait for the others before moving out, putting myself between Pell’s burden and the man remaining at the corner. “One watcher’s gone toward town,” I murmur. “Let’s keep to the busy streets.”
