scenes.narration:
Sefa lets the coin's light fall across Pell's arms and the oak box. In the shade of the gallery it shows faintly, a warm smudge on the iron. She says what she has to say about the seal in a low voice. Tyr's scales rest on a warhammer, and these have no hammer, only the shut eye. Wenna hears it from the rail.

"I'll swear to what I saw." She doesn't look round. "That wax was on that box the morning I found him, the same as it is now. What god it's meant for, I couldn't tell you. I'm not chapel."

Sefa goes to the rail at her own pace and looks down at the boy, not at the street. She gives him her message: Bram has heard, he'll come before the noon bell if the road stays clear, Mistress Brand shouldn't wait past it, and he isn't to stop and talk to anyone on the way. Pell's voice comes down the stair right after hers, louder and easy, a hireling with nothing on his mind. *Yes, before noon, at the Song.* Nothing about counting-houses, and no numbers. A copper spins down the steps, and the boy catches it against his chest with both hands.

"Long way round," the boy says back, nodding hard. "Not the smith street. Not a number." His eyes are already on the coin.

Before he goes, Sefa asks Wenna her question quietly. Have those two at the corner been round her gate before, or only since the broad man started asking?

Wenna thinks about it properly, which is more than she has done for most questions this morning. "Not before today. Him on the block I'd have noticed. He's been sat there since I put the bread in." She tightens her mouth. "The big one came on his own, both times. No friends."

Bram says his piece quietly to the other two: the Song first, together; Odda's own words before any money moves; twenty-two gold all told and not forty; and he won't tell Vell his wax is whole when they know the wax isn't Vell's. He checks that his sword sits loose in the scabbard, settles the shield and goes down the stair ahead of the box. The steps take his weight with a long creak each.

At the bottom he puts two more coppers into the boy's palm. The boy listens to him with his head tipped back: *I haven't paid yet. We're coming to the Song now. Don't tell anyone else our business.* He repeats it under his breath, adds it to what the other two said, and the three messages run together into one long sentence. Then he's off. He doesn't go out of the gate. He cuts past Tobin's barrels, down the back of the yard past the shed, and drops into the nettle lane with a yelp when the nettles get his bare shins. After that he's gone.

On the gallery Pell tells Wenna the outline in the dust is single and that she told it true. She looks at him a moment.

"I know I did." Then, when he says that anyone with Gate shoulders who asks will hear they went up the hill, she gives a short breath that is nearly a laugh. "Everybody does." She picks the bright padlock off the hasp where she'd hung it and stands aside for the box.

Pell comes down with the box square against his chest and both hands on the drop handles. Sefa comes behind him. The coin's light is still in her palm, faint in the sun, and it leans forward toward the green bead the way a candle flame leans toward an open door. Tobin rolls his finished barrel out of the gateway without being asked and goes back to his staves.

Out on the Coast Way the sun is high enough to whiten the dust. Bram takes the outside, between the box and the lane, and they walk up toward town past the yards and lodging-houses. The boy at the chandler's has finished sluicing the step. A woman is shaking out a sheet. Nobody stares.

At the corner the man on the mounting block watches them come. He's thin, with a sunburnt neck and a straw stuck in the side of his mouth, and he looks at Bram's shield the way you'd look at a dog behind a fence. When they've passed him he gets up, stretches, and comes along after them about forty feet back. He keeps to the other side of the street and stops when they stop, at a cart, a puddle or a man with a barrow.

The smithy street takes them in with its noise. The forges are going full now. Hammer on hammer comes out of every open front, and the air shakes with heat above the quench-tubs. Further up, toward the turn for the hill and the Song, a Fist trooper is leaning in the same doorway as before. He's awake this time and paring his nails with a knife.

Between the trooper and the three of them, a pair of broad shoulders comes down the middle of the street.

He has no apple this time. He's a big man in a brown leather jerkin, bareheaded, his hair cut close. He walks the way a man walks on a street he has already paid for, not hurrying, and people step round him without noticing they've done it. Half a pace behind him and to the side is the man from the wall. He has seen what he was sent to see, and now he's watching it come up the hill. The broad man's eyes go over Bram's shield and Sefa's open hand without stopping, and come to rest on the oak box in Pell's arms. He doesn't slow down. Behind them the man with the straw has stopped walking. He's leaning on a smithy's doorpost, forty feet back, and he isn't looking at anything at all.

 (Out of game: none of the four needed a roll. Sefa already knew Tyr's mark from her temple training, as established last round, and the other three were plain words and a coin that nobody resisted, so each happened as declared and is told above.)

You stay on the sill and call down to the boy, loud and easy, then give him a copper and send him the long way round. Sefa meanwhile lets the coin's light fall across you and the oak box, a faint warm smudge on the iron in the shade of the gallery. She says in a low voice that the seal can't be Tyr's, since his mark has a warhammer under the scales, and this one has scales and a shut eye and no hammer. Wenna, at the rail, says she'll swear the wax was on the box the morning she found him, just as it is now, though she can't say what god it's meant for, not being chapel.

Sefa goes to the rail and tells the boy that Bram has heard, that Bram will come before the noon bell provided the road is clear, that his mistress shouldn't wait past it, and that he's to talk to no one on the way. Your coin spins down the steps and the boy catches it against his chest. He says back that it's the long way round, not the smith street, not a number, with his eyes already on the coin.

Sefa asks Wenna whether the two at the corner have been round her gate before. Wenna thinks about it properly. Not before today, she says. The one on the block has sat there since she put the bread in, and the big man came on his own both times, with no friends.

You lay out your changed plan to the other two. Bram says Song first, together: Odda's own words before any money moves, twenty-two gold and not forty, and he won't tell Vell the wax is whole when it isn't Vell's. He checks his sword, settles his shield and goes down the long-creaking stair ahead of the box. At the bottom he puts two more coppers in the boy's palm and tells him that he hasn't paid yet, that you're coming to the Song now, and that he's to tell no one else. The boy mutters it over, his three messages run into one long sentence, and he's off. He cuts past Tobin's barrels and down the back of the yard, drops into the nettle lane with a yelp when the nettles get his shins, and vanishes.

You tell Wenna that the outline in the dust is single and she told it true. She says she knows she did, and when you add that anyone with Gate shoulders who asks will hear you went up the hill, she lets out a short, nearly laughing breath. Everybody does, she says. She takes the bright padlock off the hasp and stands aside. You come down with the box square against your chest and both hands on the drop handles, Sefa behind you. The coin's light in her palm is faint in the sun and leans toward the green bead like a candle flame toward an open door. Tobin rolls his finished barrel out of the gateway unasked.

On the Coast Way the sun whitens the dust. Bram takes the outside, between the box and the lane. Nobody stares. At the corner the thin, sunburnt man on the mounting block, a straw in his mouth, watches you come and looks at Bram's shield as you'd look at a dog behind a fence. When you've passed he gets up and follows about forty feet back on the other side of the street, stopping when you stop.

The smithy street swallows you in noise and heat from the forges. Up toward the turn for the hill and the Song, a Fist trooper leans in the same doorway as before, awake now and paring his nails with a knife. Between him and you, the broad man comes down the middle of the street in his brown leather jerkin, bareheaded, hair close-cut, no apple this time. People step round him without noticing. The man from the wall is half a pace behind him. The broad man's eyes pass over Bram's shield and Sefa's open hand and settle on the box in your arms. He doesn't slow. Behind you the man with the straw has stopped and leans on a smithy doorpost, looking at nothing.

relay.request:
Characters at the table: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.
In this scene: Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway.
Write the screens of, in this order: Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Sefa Marrin: Sefa lets the coin's light fall across Pell and the oak box, and keeps her voice low. "Before we move that another step, the seal is not Tyr's. His mark is scales over a warhammer. This has the scales and a blind eye, but no hammer. Either someone borrowed the god's look, or they stamped it not knowing the difference. That's worth saying aloud now, while Wenna can still swear no one's tampered with it."

She crosses to the gallery rail without hurrying, looking down at the boy rather than out at the street. "Tell your mistress Bram has heard her message, and he'll come before the noon bell if the road stays clear. Tell her not to wait past it, and don't stop to talk to anyone else along the way."

Then, more quietly, to Bram as he moves to the stair: "Go by the busiest lane. If you glance back, do it for traffic, not for pursuers." She turns her head toward Wenna. "Those two out there—one by the wall, one on the mounting block. Have they been round your gate before, or only since the broad man came asking?"

Pell Dunmore: Pell doesn't move off the sill, but his voice comes down the stair before Bram's can, easy and loud enough for the yard — the voice of a hireling with nothing on his mind.

"Boy. The big man's heard you. Tell Mistress Brand *yes, before noon, at the Song.* Nothing else — not the counting-house, not a number. You've said forty once in a cooper's yard already and that's once too often." He shifts the box onto one hip just long enough to fish a copper out and flip it down the stair to him. "That's for the running. Go the long way round the smith street. There's a man walking up it ahead of you and I'd rather he didn't hear what you're carrying."

Then, low, to the other two on the gallery, his back to the lane: "Change of plan, and a small one. That boy just told half the Coast Way that Bram's got business at Vell's counter about forty gold, and the one by the wall took a good look at this box and walked off toward town the moment he heard it. So Bram doesn't go to Vell's alone — not now, not with Thale's man knowing his name and his errand. We all go up to the Song. Odda's at the almshouse door till the noon bell; Bram talks to her there with his own ears, Sefa asks for Brother Aldane, and I sit in the porch with Lathander's doorkeeper and this on my knees. Vell gets his box at dusk like he said. He doesn't get it a minute sooner."

He glances at Sefa. "And you're right about the hammer. I jumped. Scales with no hammer and a shut eye — that's not Tyr's house, that's somebody who wanted it to *look* like a court's seal to anyone who didn't grow up next to a temple. Which means Jassan didn't go to a notary. He went to somebody private. The old brother might know who stamps lead in this town."

Last, to Wenna, as he steps onto the gallery and makes room for Bram to take the stair: "One outline in the dust, Mistress Pike. He set it down once and never lifted it again. You told it true." A nod. "If anyone with Gate shoulders asks, we went up the hill. Everyone goes up the hill."

He waits for Bram's shield to be one step below him, then follows, the box held square and both hands on the handles, Sefa behind with her light put away.

Bram Halloway: “Song first, together,” I tell Pell and Sefa quietly. “Odda’s there, and I need to hear the rest before buying anything. I’ve twenty-two gold all told, not forty. And I won’t tell Vell his wax is whole when we know it isn’t his.”

I check that my sword is loose in its scabbard, shield ready, then take the stairs ahead of Pell, watching the gate.

At the bottom I give the boy two copper. “Thank you. Tell Mistress Brand I haven’t paid yet. We’re coming to the Song now. Don’t tell anyone else our business if they ask.”

I wait for the others before moving out, putting myself between Pell’s burden and the man remaining at the corner. “One watcher’s gone toward town,” I murmur. “Let’s keep to the busy streets.”
>>>

Before he goes, Sefa asks Wenna her question quietly. Have those two at the corner been round her gate before, or only since the broad man started asking?

Wenna thinks about it properly, which is more than she has done for most questions this morning. "Not before today. Him on the block I'd have noticed. He's been sat there since I put the bread in." She tightens her mouth. "The big one came on his own, both times. No friends."

Bram says his piece quietly to the other two: the Song first, together; Odda's own words before any money moves; twenty-two gold all told and not forty; and he won't tell Vell his wax is whole when they know the wax isn't Vell's. He checks that his sword sits loose in the scabbard, settles the shield and goes down the stair ahead of the box. The steps take his weight with a long creak each.

At the bottom he puts two more coppers into the boy's palm. The boy listens to him with his head tipped back: *I haven't paid yet. We're coming to the Song now. Don't tell anyone else our business.* He repeats it under his breath, adds it to what the other two said, and the three messages run together into one long sentence. Then he's off. He doesn't go out of the gate. He cuts past Tobin's barrels, down the back of the yard past the shed, and drops into the nettle lane with a yelp when the nettles get his bare shins. After that he's gone.

On the gallery Pell tells Wenna the outline in the dust is single and that she told it true. She looks at him a moment.

"I know I did." Then, when he says that anyone with Gate shoulders who asks will hear they went up the hill, she gives a short breath that is nearly a laugh. "Everybody does." She picks the bright padlock off the hasp where she'd hung it and stands aside for the box.

Pell comes down with the box square against his chest and both hands on the drop handles. Sefa comes behind him. The coin's light is still in her palm, faint in the sun, and it leans forward toward the green bead the way a candle flame leans toward an open door. Tobin rolls his finished barrel out of the gateway without being asked and goes back to his staves.

Out on the Coast Way the sun is high enough to whiten the dust. Bram takes the outside, between the box and the lane, and they walk up toward town past the yards and lodging-houses. The boy at the chandler's has finished sluicing the step. A woman is shaking out a sheet. Nobody stares.

At the corner the man on the mounting block watches them come. He's thin, with a sunburnt neck and a straw stuck in the side of his mouth, and he looks at Bram's shield the way you'd look at a dog behind a fence. When they've passed him he gets up, stretches, and comes along after them about forty feet back. He keeps to the other side of the street and stops when they stop, at a cart, a puddle or a man with a barrow.

The smithy street takes them in with its noise. The forges are going full now. Hammer on hammer comes out of every open front, and the air shakes with heat above the quench-tubs. Further up, toward the turn for the hill and the Song, a Fist trooper is leaning in the same doorway as before. He's awake this time and paring his nails with a knife.

Between the trooper and the three of them, a pair of broad shoulders comes down the middle of the street.

He has no apple this time. He's a big man in a brown leather jerkin, bareheaded, his hair cut close. He walks the way a man walks on a street he has already paid for, not hurrying, and people step round him without noticing they've done it. Half a pace behind him and to the side is the man from the wall. He has seen what he was sent to see, and now he's watching it come up the hill. The broad man's eyes go over Bram's shield and Sefa's open hand without stopping, and come to rest on the oak box in Pell's arms. He doesn't slow down. Behind them the man with the straw has stopped walking. He's leaning on a smithy's doorpost, forty feet back, and he isn't looking at anything at all.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't break stride and doesn't shift the box. His grip stays on the drop handles; his eyes stay on the broad man's hands, not his face.

Low, for Bram and Sefa only: "Don't stop and don't speed up. Bram, shield-side to him and half a pace ahead of me. Sefa, my other side. We walk straight at the trooper in the doorway like he's an old friend — I want this said within ten feet of a Fist uniform, not twenty." A beat. "If he wants to talk, let me. He's Gate. I know what that sounds like."

When the broad man comes level — or stops in front of them — Pell gives him the kind of nod one Lower City man gives another on a strange street: neither friendly nor not. And as his left hand resettles on the handle, two fingers tap the iron corner in a small, plain rhythm — the Cant's shrug: *hired, not freelancing, nothing here's yours.* He watches whether the man's eyes flick to it.

Aloud, pitched easy, Gate vowels coming back into it without effort: "Morning. You'll be Coll. Thale's man." Civil. "You've got your master's coin and I've got mine. Box goes to the name on the brass. Thale wants to read Vell's books, he can go to Vell's counter and bid like a gentleman, or he can wait for the Fist to want to read them, which—" a glance at the trooper's doorway, not hidden, "—from the look of things is going to happen sooner than he'd like. Either way it's not a street matter. Not in the smiths' street at midmorning with Lathander's bell going." He lets a half-step go by. "I'd put it to him that way. You've been paid to carry a box, not to start a thing. So have I."

He keeps walking toward the doorway and the trooper's knife, and doesn't look back for the man with the straw. Bram can tell him if the straw moves.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Keep close. Don’t let the one behind get at the box,” I say quietly.

I move between Pell and the broad man, staying within a shield’s reach of Pell. My sword stays sheathed. I leave the man room to pass, but no straight path to the strongbox.

“Morning. If you’re after Mistress Pike’s room, we’ve already settled the rent.”

I speak clearly enough for the nearby trooper to hear. “We’re carrying this on Ostrin Vell’s written authority. What’s your business?”

I watch his hands as I address him, shield ready to protect Pell if either man attacks.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't slow. She moves half a step to Pell's other side, so she and Bram bracket the box, and sets her free hand lightly on Pell's arm, not to pull him back but to keep their stride together. To Bram she says, low and even, "Don't stop. Shield side to them. Don't let them turn us down a lane."

Then she raises her voice, and something in it gathers the way a struck bell gathers sound—not a shout, but a carrying voice, as if the air itself had leaned in to listen. Her coin burns brighter in her palm.

"Coll Brannock! If that's you, move aside. We carry a dead man's strongbox under seal to the Song, in broad morning, with witnesses from the yard to the corner. If your master wants lawful words about it, he can meet us at the temple steps and say them in front of the god's own door. But you won't take it here."

Her eyes stay on the broad man's hands, not his face. She keeps her voice pitched to the street, so the smiths and the Fist trooper can't pretend they didn't hear. She doesn't reach for her dagger. The light in her palm doesn't waver.

scenes.narration:
Pell keeps walking. Bram moves half a pace ahead on the shield side, between the box and the middle of the street. Sefa comes up on Pell's other side and rests her free hand lightly on his arm, so the three of them walk in step. The trooper's doorway is about sixty feet up the hill and getting closer.

The broad man doesn't step into their way. He drifts toward them across the street at the same unhurried pace, and the man from the wall drifts with him, until all five of them meet beside a smithy's open front with a quench-tub steaming at the door. Pell gives him the plain nod of one Lower City man to another. His left hand resettles on the drop handle, and two fingers tap the iron corner in a quick, flat rhythm.

The broad man's eyes go down to the fingers and come straight back up. He read it. He hooks a thumb into his belt and taps the buckle twice with his forefinger, an old, lazy Wide answer: *heard. Business, not blades.* Then he looks at Pell's face for longer than he has looked at anything else this morning. It isn't hostile. He looks at Pell like a man trying to place a door he walked past once, years ago.

Bram's voice comes over the hammering, clear enough to carry to the doorway: the rent is settled, the box goes on Ostrin Vell's written authority, so what is his business? The broad man turns his head to Bram without hurry.

"Settled. I heard." His voice is low, with Gate vowels flattened by years of somewhere else. "Mistress Pike's square. Good for her."

Then Sefa raises her voice.

It doesn't sound like shouting. The air in the street seems to lean in toward her and give her words back three times as loud. The nearest hammer stops in mid-stroke. In her palm the coin flares bright enough to throw a shadow from Pell's wrist onto the oak. *Coll Brannock.* The name rolls up the smithy street and down it again. *A dead man's strongbox under seal… witnesses from the yard to the corner… the temple steps… you won't take it here.*

The smith at the quench-tub stands holding his tongs and stares at them. Up the hill the trooper pushes off his doorpost, folds his knife shut and puts it away. He doesn't come down. He just stands where they can all see him, watching.

Coll shuts his eyes for half a heartbeat, the face of a man who has just heard his own name shouted in a street he meant to walk through quietly. Then he lets out a breath through his nose and leans one shoulder on the smithy's doorpost, as comfortably as if he'd been invited.

"No call for trouble." He says it to Sefa, and it's quieter than anything else on the street now. "Nobody's taking anything. I came to talk."

He turns back to Pell, and he speaks to him the way you'd speak to someone from the same street.

"You said it fair. Hired. So am I." He nods at the box without reaching for it. "So here's my hire. Thale pays sixty gold for that, as it sits, wax and all. Eighty if the three of you walk it down to his counting-room yourselves and tell him to his face where it came from and who sealed it." His eyes go to the green bead and stay there. "He's had a look at that wax through Mistress Pike's door this week, same as you. He knows it isn't Vell's."

He lets a cart go by. "You want to know why Thale wants it, I'll tell you what he told me. Three, four men who owed Vell went down the Way to Nashkel this year and didn't come back. Wagons and all. Thale wants to know why Vell's debtors don't come home. Maybe you'd want to know too, before you put it on Vell's counter." He shrugs one shoulder against the post. "That's all. That's the offer."

To Bram he gives a short nod, nearly polite. "Your business is the box. Mine too. Nobody here wants it done in the street."

Then he looks at Sefa again, and the corner of his mouth moves. "Temple steps suit me. Lathander doesn't mind a man naming a price." journal: Thread: Thale's offer for the box

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Bring the missing men’s names, Coll. Their wagons, when they left, who reported them missing. Something we can check. An offer of coin tells us what Thale wants, not whether he’s right.”

I keep walking with Pell and Sefa, watching our follower whenever the street turns.

Quietly, to the others: “I’ve guarded that road for years. Those names might mean something to me. We hear him out at the Song, but we don’t sell him another man’s box.”

As we pass the trooper, I give him a civil nod. “Morning. Is Sergeant Cowl on duty at the market post today?” I don’t stop or draw away from Pell.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the carrying edge go out of her voice, and the light in her palm dims until it is only a warm coin again. She keeps walking, not looking back.

"Then sit on the steps, Coll. You'll get your answer where the god can hear it." She pitches the next words for Pell and Bram alone. "The Song first, as planned. Bram hears Odda with his own ears; I ask Brother Aldane about the vial. And we keep the box between us the whole while." A beat. "The tale about Vell's debtors to Nashkel may be true and still not be his to buy. I won't hand a dead man's books to whoever pays most by noon."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps walking. The box doesn't shift.

To Coll, over his shoulder, same street voice: "Eighty's a good number for a thing that isn't mine to sell. Tell your master I heard it. And I heard *Nashkel.*" A nod, nothing more. "Temple steps. In the sun."

Then, low, to the other two as the smithy falls behind: "Well. That's three parties who want this box and two of them say the wax isn't Vell's. Thale's man just told us Vell's debtors go down the Way to Nashkel and don't come back — and the Fist's got caravans vanishing between Beregost and Nashkel that nobody can account for. If that's one story and not two, then Jassan wasn't writing to Cowl about double-sold paper. He was writing about *men.*" He breathes out through his nose. "I still don't sell what I was hired to carry. Not for eighty, not on the street. But I'm no longer sure the man I carry it *to* gets to open it alone behind his counter either."

He glances at Sefa. "That was well done, the shouting. Loud is safe. I'd forgotten." A flicker of a smile. "Don't make a habit of it around me."

They reach the trooper's doorway. Pell slows there — doesn't stop, just lets the box rest on his hip a moment, as a tired porter might — and speaks to the Fist man as to a neighbour, Gate vowels still in his mouth. "Morning. scenes.narration:
Bram speaks without slowing. Coll keeps pace at the edge of the street, a cart's width off, and hears him out with his eyes on the forges.

"Names." He says the word as if he were weighing it. "Names are Thale's stock, not mine. He sells them, I don't." They walk a few steps. "One you get free, since you asked like a man who's been on that road. Past the Lionsfang ford. Go to the Jovial Juggler and ask who's been drinking on the slate since his wagons didn't come home. He'll tell you the rest himself if you buy the cup." His mouth moves at one corner. "Who reported them? The Fist wrote them down. Ask your sergeant what he did with the paper after."

Sefa lets the carrying edge go out of her voice. The street gives her words back at their own size now, and the light in her palm dims to a warm coin. She tells Coll to sit on the steps, that he'll get his answer where the god can hear it, and Coll dips his head to her, nearly a bow. When she drops her voice for the other two, he's already falling back.

Pell's words go over his shoulder in the same street voice: eighty is a good number, *Nashkel*, temple steps in the sun. Coll answers that one to Pell and nobody else.

"Steps, then." He looks at Pell's face again, the same way as before, a man placing an old door. Then he peels off with the man from the wall into an alley between two smithies. It's barely wide enough for his shoulders. They're gone before the next hammer falls.

Bram's quiet word to the others and Pell's low reckoning pass between the three of them under the noise of the forges. Behind them, on the far side of the street, the man with the straw walks when they walk.

At the doorway the trooper has his thumbs in his belt. He's young, with a peeling nose and a Fist tabard that has been washed too often. Bram gives him a civil nod and asks after Sergeant Cowl. A few strides later Pell slows by him with the box on his hip and asks the same thing in Gate vowels, and adds the rest: a dead clerk's box, three prices on it, and he'd sooner the Fist knew where it slept tonight.

The trooper looks from the shield to the box and then down the hill, where the alley swallowed Coll.

"Cowl's at the market post till the noon muster. You'll hear him before you see him." He scratches his nose. "A box isn't Fist business till somebody bleeds on it." He thinks about that and adds, quieter, "Tell Cowl anyway. He collects talk about the Way. Nobody pays him for that either." Then he leans back into his doorway and watches the street, the man with the straw included.

The turn for the hill takes them out of the heat. The street climbs between garden walls, and the hammering drops behind until it's only a ringing. The Song of the Morning stands on the crest, rose-coloured stone with its gilded sunburst catching the full sun over the doors. A wide forecourt of swept flags lies in front of it, with a fountain chuckling in the middle. Two novices in saffron are scrubbing the fountain's lip and arguing about whose turn it is to fetch the lye.

Coll Brannock is already on the temple steps. He's sitting three steps up, leaning on a pillar's base with his legs out, as though he'd been there an hour. The man from the wall sits two pillars along. Neither of them is out of breath.

At the forecourt gate the man with the straw stops and finds a wall to lean on.

To the left of the great doors a low side door stands open on a whitewashed passage, with a bench beside it. Seven or eight people wait there in a ragged line: a carter with a bandaged hand, two old men, a girl with a baby. One woman stands a little apart from the line in a grey shawl, with her hands clasped hard at her waist. Beside her, still barefoot, with nettle welts on his shins, Odda's runner sees the shield come through the gate and points at it with his whole arm.

In the passage behind them a brother in saffron moves among the bench and the doorways with a basin. Up in the bell tower the rope hangs still. The noon bell is a good two hours off.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.text:
Sefa crosses the forecourt at an easy, unhurried pace, and as they near the fountain, she looks once at the boy with the nettle welts. "Hold still a moment," she says, not unkindly, and crouches to brush a bit of leaf from the boy's shin—no healing, just the habit of a hospice sister checking a child's scrapes. The gesture is brief, and she straightens without making much of it.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes the forecourt in the way he took the street: fountain, two novices, the queue, the side passage, Coll three steps up with his legs out, the straw-man finding his wall. Then he picks his ground.

Not the steps. Coll chose the steps; Pell won't share them with a man who wants his box. He goes instead to the side door, to the end of the ragged line, and finds the brother with the basin when he comes near.

"Brother. Three of us, on an errand that's turned heavier than it was at breakfast." He lifts the box an inch to show it. "A dead man's strongbox, sealed, that I'm sworn to carry unopened to the man it belongs to at dusk. Between now and then there's two men on your steps and one on your gate who'd like to carry it elsewhere. I'd ask leave to sit inside your door with it on my knees — the passage, the porch, wherever your doorkeeper can see me and the god can too. I'll touch nothing and I'll bother no one. The lady's a hospice novice from the Gate; she'll want a word with Brother Aldane, about Jassan Ferr's medicine — he knew the man. The big one has business with the woman in the grey shawl, and she's come a long way to say it." He adds a silver to the basin, not making a show of it. "For the fountain lye, since they're arguing over it."

To Bram and Sefa, low, before they part: "I'll be in that doorway with the box in sight of both of you. Bram — hear Odda out, but don't put coin in anyone's hand until the three of us have talked. If she says Jassan told her the debt would be called *once the box came back*, ask her what he said would happen if it didn't. Sefa — the vial, the half-sun tag, and one thing more: ask the old brother who in Beregost stamps lead under wax. Scales and a shut eye. A town this size has one man who does that, and a temple knows who."

Then, as he settles on the bench inside the door with the oak square on his knees and his back to the whitewash, he looks out through the opening at Coll on the steps, and raises his chin a quarter inch — *I see you; I'm not coming over.* He lets Coll stew in the sun a while. A man who's been paid to wait can wait.

And he watches the straw-man at the gate, because the straw-man isn't Coll's. Coll came with one friend, both times. The straw-man was at the corner before any of them, and he's the only one who hasn't been introduced.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I lead us toward the woman in the grey shawl, keeping clear of the patients’ line.

“Odda? Bram Halloway. I got your letter. These are Sefa and Pell; they’re carrying this responsibility with me, and I’ve told them what you wrote.”

I lower my voice so it won’t carry to the steps.

“I haven’t paid Vell yet. Tell me the rest—what did Jassan say would happen when the box was opened? And have you his letter, or any papers about Harl’s debt?”

I stay beside Pell rather than draw Odda away alone. “We can ask for somewhere private if you’d rather.”

scenes.narration:
Sefa crosses the forecourt at her own pace. By the fountain she crouches in front of the runner and tells him to hold still. He does, stiffly, the way children hold still for people with basins. She picks a nettle leaf off his shin and stands up again. The boy looks down at his leg, then at her, and decides he doesn't mind.

The three of them make their arrangements in a few low words. Then Sefa goes to the side door with her hands folded and her beads showing over her knuckles. Pell gets there at almost the same moment, walking along the back of the line with the box held square.

The brother with the basin is about fifty and thick in the waist. His sleeves are rolled to the elbow and wet to the elbow. He hears Sefa out, then Pell, without putting the basin down.

"Aldane's in the still-room. He makes up the drops." He tips his head back down the whitewashed passage, toward somewhere that smells of boiled herbs. "Paulin!" One of the fountain novices looks up. "Go and tell Brother Aldane a lady from a Gate hospice wants him at the door. About Jassan Ferr." The novice puts his brush down and goes in at a trot, plainly glad of the excuse.

Pell's silver goes into the basin. The brother looks at it lying among the coppers.

"Lye's a copper a pail. The rest goes to the line." He raises his voice slightly toward the fountain. "It's paid for. Both of you scrub." The second novice shuts his mouth on whatever he was going to say. Then the brother looks at the box and at Pell. "Sit at the end of the bench, inside. Nobody takes anything off that bench. I'm in and out of this door all morning, and so's the god. I'm not a strongroom, and this isn't one. Don't let me find a fight in my passage."

Pell sits at the inner end of the bench, his back against the cool whitewash and the oak square on his knees. Through the doorway he has the steps, the fountain and the gate. He looks at Coll and lifts his chin a quarter of an inch.

Coll sees it. He doesn't get up. He lifts two fingers off his knee as if waving away a fly. At the forecourt gate the man with the straw pushes off his wall and strolls along the inside of the forecourt wall, until he's leaning again thirty feet nearer, where the side door is in plain view. He doesn't look at Coll while he does it. He doesn't have to. Pell saw the fingers move first and the man move after.

Bram goes to the woman in the grey shawl, keeping clear of the line. Up close she's forty or so, weathered across the cheekbones, with a carter's wife's hands, broad and rough. She hears his name, then Sefa's and Pell's, and looks at the box on Pell's knees for a long moment.

When he offers somewhere private she glances once at the steps, at Coll's outstretched legs, and steps in over the threshold of the side door. That puts her an arm's length from Pell's bench and out of the steps' line of sight.

"Here's private enough. Everyone on that bench owes somebody." She keeps her hands clasped at her waist. "I was on the step across from Vell's this morning. I'd been in to ask him for time and he said no. I heard you through his window, asking if anybody would dispute his claim. I thought, that one listens. So I wrote to you."

She answers his question plainly. "Jassan never said *opened*. He said *goes back*." She takes a folded paper from inside her shawl and puts it into Bram's hand to read, but she doesn't let go of it with her eyes. "That's all I've got. Harl never had a copy of his note. Men like Harl don't."

The hand is small and even, a clerk's, the same from line to line:

*Mistress Brand — I am sorry for Harl. His note for forty is among the books I have locked up here. When they go back to the counter it will be entered with the rest, and the master means to call every account on the Way the day after. Before that it can be bought back at its face, at the counter, by whoever pays. Do not wait until it is opened. I can do nothing more for you than tell you this. I have done enough with my pen. — J. Ferr*

"Harl borrowed it in the spring for a wagon and a pair of mules," Odda says while Bram reads. "He drove for Dobbin. Down to Nashkel with iron goods. They didn't come back past the Lionsfang ford, not Harl or the mules or the other three drivers. No bodies. In the summer the Fist wrote all four of them down as dead, so dead's what I'm called now." Her jaw sets. "Dobbin's at the Juggler, drinking on the slate. He'll tell you he's sorry. He tells everybody." She stops there, because that's all she meant to say.

Inside the passage, past the bench and the basin and the smell of herbs, a stick taps slowly on the flags. It stops, taps again and comes on. Paulin walks half a pace ahead and keeps having to wait. Behind him comes an old man in saffron, bald as an egg, one hand on the stick and the other on the wall. His eyes find Sefa in the doorway, then move to the oak box on Pell's knees, and he slows down even more.

Out on the steps, Coll has tilted his face to the sun and shut his eyes.

She picks a nettle leaf off his shin and stands up again. The boy looks down at his leg, then at her, and decides he doesn't mind.

The three of them make their arrangements in a few low words. Then Sefa goes to the side door with her hands folded and her beads showing over her knuckles. Pell gets there at almost the same moment, walking along the back of the line with the box held square.

The brother with the basin is about fifty and thick in the waist. His sleeves are rolled to the elbow and wet to the elbow. He hears Sefa out, then Pell, without putting the basin down.

"Aldane's in the still-room. He makes up the drops." He tips his head back down the whitewashed passage, toward somewhere that smells of boiled herbs. "Paulin!" One of the fountain novices looks up. "Go and tell Brother Aldane a lady from a Gate hospice wants him at the door. About Jassan Ferr." The novice puts his brush down and goes in at a trot, plainly glad of the excuse.

Pell's silver goes into the basin. The brother looks at it lying among the coppers.

"Lye's a copper a pail. The rest goes to the line." He raises his voice slightly toward the fountain. "It's paid for. Both of you scrub." The second novice shuts his mouth on whatever he was going to say. Then the brother looks at the box and at Pell. "Sit at the end of the bench, inside. Nobody takes anything off that bench. I'm in and out of this door all morning, and so's the god. I'm not a strongroom, and this isn't one. Don't let me find a fight in my passage."

Pell sits at the inner end of the bench, his back against the cool whitewash and the oak square on his knees. Through the doorway he has the steps, the fountain and the gate. He looks at Coll and lifts his chin a quarter of an inch.

Coll sees it. He doesn't get up. He lifts two fingers off his knee as if waving away a fly. At the forecourt gate the man with the straw pushes off his wall and strolls along the inside of the forecourt wall, until he's leaning again thirty feet nearer, where the side door is in plain view. He doesn't look at Coll while he does it. He doesn't have to. Pell saw the fingers move first and the man move after.

Bram goes to the woman in the grey shawl, keeping clear of the line. Up close she's forty or so, weathered across the cheekbones, with a carter's wife's hands, broad and rough. She hears his name, then Sefa's and Pell's, and looks at the box on Pell's knees for a long moment.

When he offers somewhere private she glances once at the steps, at Coll's outstretched legs, and steps in over the threshold of the side door. That puts her an arm's length from Pell's bench and out of the steps' line of sight.

"Here's private enough. Everyone on that bench owes somebody." She keeps her hands clasped at her waist. "I was on the step across from Vell's this morning. I'd been in to ask him for time and he said no. I heard you through his window, asking if anybody would dispute his claim. I thought, that one listens. So I wrote to you."

She answers his question plainly. "Jassan never said *opened*. He said *goes back*." She takes a folded paper from inside her shawl and puts it into Bram's hand to read, but she doesn't let go of it with her eyes. "That's all I've got. Harl never had a copy of his note. Men like Harl don't."

The hand is small and even, a clerk's, the same from line to line:

*Mistress Brand — I am sorry for Harl. His note for forty is among the books I have locked up here. When they go back to the counter it will be entered with the rest, and the master means to call every account on the Way the day after. Before that it can be bought back at its face, at the counter, by whoever pays. Do not wait until it is opened. I can do nothing more for you than tell you this. I have done enough with my pen. — J. Ferr*

"Harl borrowed it in the spring for a wagon and a pair of mules," Odda says while Bram reads. "He drove for Dobbin. Down to Nashkel with iron goods. They didn't come back past the Lionsfang ford, not Harl or the mules or the other three drivers. No bodies. In the summer the Fist wrote all four of them down as dead, so dead's what I'm called now." Her jaw sets. "Dobbin's at the Juggler, drinking on the slate. He'll tell you he's sorry. He tells everybody." She stops there, because that's all she meant to say.

Inside the passage, past the bench and the basin and the smell of herbs, a stick taps slowly on the flags. It stops, taps again and comes on. Paulin walks half a pace ahead and keeps having to wait. Behind him comes an old man in saffron, bald as an egg, one hand on the stick and the other on the wall. His eyes find Sefa in the doorway, then move to the oak box on Pell's knees, and he slows down even more.

Out on the steps, Coll has tilted his face to the sun and shut his eyes.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't get up. He keeps the oak square on his knees and his hands on the handles, and watches the old man come down the passage — not the stick, not the bald head, but the eyes, and where they stop. They stopped on the box before they stopped on the novice from the Gate. He files that.

Low, to Bram, without turning his head: "The straw's Coll's after all. Two fingers off the knee and the man moved. So Thale's got three on us, not two, and he lets us count wrong on purpose. Mind that when you talk prices."

Then to Odda, quiet, neighbour to neighbour, his eyes still on the passage: "Mistress Brand. One thing, and I'm not Vell's and I'm not the Fist. The paper Harl signed in the spring — did you see it? Was there wax on it, and under the wax a little grey disc of lead? Round mark, scales, an eye shut?" He waits for her face more than her words. "And Dobbin's wagons — did Dobbin borrow from Vell too, or only your Harl? Because if every driver who went past the Lionsfang ford this year had Vell's paper on his house first, then the road didn't eat them. The ledger did."

He lets Sefa take Brother Aldane; it's her ground and her beads. But as the old man draws level with the bench, Pell shifts the box an inch so the green bead on the hasp catches the light from the door — nothing pointed, a porter easing a weight — and says, mild, looking up: "Brother. You knew Jassan Ferr by sight, Mistress Pike says. You picked up his bottle, smelled it, and said *heart*." A beat, no edge in it. "I've got the bottle in my bag. I'd like you to smell it again. In front of the lady."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’m sorry, Odda. No bodies is a hard way to be told you’re a widow.”

I read Jassan’s note once more, then offer it back. “May Sefa and Pell read this too? It ties Harl’s loss to the missing wagons we’ve just heard about.”

I keep my voice low. “Did Harl pledge the house when he borrowed, or is that what Vell told you afterward? And did Jassan ever explain what he meant by ‘done enough with my pen’?”

To Pell, quietly: “Same ford. Same Dobbin at the Juggler. That part of Coll’s story holds.”

I make room for the old brother to reach Sefa, keeping Pell and the box close. “I have twenty-two gold to put toward buying the note. Before I ask either of you for the rest, let’s hear what Brother Aldane knows.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps aside from the doorway so the old brother can pass, and bows her head a little—not a temple bow, but the nod of one who once wore the same kind of saffron work. "Brother Aldane. I'm Sefa Marrin. I used to keep a ward in the Lower City, so I know the smell of a still-room and the sound of a man being too polite about his knees. Thank you for coming out."

She walks with him as far as Pell's bench, close enough that all three of them can speak low and still keep the box in view. "We won't keep you long. Three days ago you were called down to the Coast Way for Jassan Ferr. I'd like to hear, plainly, what you found that made you say *heart* so certain. And this—" She turns to Pell, indicating the satchel. "The little brown vial with your house's half-sun. Was that something made here, and what would it be? It has a bitter green smell, like stems left too long in water. A man with a weak heart might take such a thing. Or be given it."

She folds her hands again. "There's a second matter, if you know it. The box carries a lead seal under green wax: scales and a shut eye, but no hammer. That isn't Tyr's stamp. You've served this town through too many quarrels not to know who presses a private seal like that in Beregost."

scenes.narration:
Pell stays where he is. The box sits square on his knees and his hands stay on the drop handles. He watches the old man coming down the passage, and mostly he watches where the old man's eyes go. Without turning his head he tells Bram that the straw man belongs to Coll, so it's three of them, and that Coll let them count wrong on purpose. Bram hears him and gives a small nod.

Bram speaks to Odda first. "I'm sorry, Odda. No bodies is a hard way to be told you're a widow."

"That's the Fist's word." She keeps her eyes on the paper in his hand. "Not mine."

He reads Jassan's note once more and holds it out to give back, then asks whether Sefa and Pell may read it too. Odda looks at each of them. She looks longest at Pell, who has his hands full of oak.

"Where I can see it."

Bram holds it open at chest height for the other two, and Odda's eyes follow it the whole time. Then the questions come, Pell's and Bram's close together, and she takes them in the order she likes.

"I saw it signed. I stood at the counter beside him in the spring and watched him make his mark. Harl doesn't write." She shakes her head at Pell. "Red wax. Vell's ring, the key. No lead, no eye. Just Vell's." To Bram: "The house went in it. Vell's clerk read it out and Harl said yes to every word. That's what pledged means, isn't it. I was there."

Pell asks about Dobbin and she answers him straight. "Dobbin had Vell's money in every wagon he ran. Harl said so. He said Dobbin owed worse than we did, and he laughed about it, because what could Dobbin do but keep driving." Her mouth sets. "The other three drivers, I couldn't tell you who they borrowed from. Ask Dobbin. He keeps count of what he's lost."

Bram asks about *done enough with my pen*. She takes longer over that one.

"He never said. He came to my door once, after the Fist wrote Harl down. Stood on the step with his hat in his hands and wouldn't come in. He said he was sorry, and that he was the one who wrote the sums. Then he went." She looks at the note. "I thought he meant he was sorry for writing Harl's loan. Now I don't know what he meant."

Bram tells Pell quietly that the ford and Dobbin at the Juggler match, so that part of Coll's story holds. Then he says it plainly: he has twenty-two gold to put toward the note, and he wants to hear Brother Aldane before he asks the other two for the rest.

Odda's clasped hands tighten at her waist until the knuckles go pale. She says nothing. *Twenty-two* sits there in the passage between them, and she leaves it there.

The stick taps the last few flags. Paulin gets to the door, sees there's no more running to be had, and goes back to the fountain and the lye. Sefa steps aside out of the doorway. She bows her head, the nod of someone who has carried basins down a ward, and gives her name and her old work.

Brother Aldane looks at her properly. He is very old. The skin of his scalp is spotted like an egg in a nest, and the hand on the stick is all knuckle. "A ward in the Lower City. Then you know how much of this work is standing about while people decide what they want to ask." Something moves at the corner of his mouth. "My knees thank you for being quick about it."

He lets her walk him the last few feet to Pell's bench. Pell eases the box an inch, the way a porter eases a weight, and the green bead on the hasp catches the light from the door. Aldane's eyes go to it and stay there. Pell says, without any edge, that the brother picked up the bottle, smelled it and said *heart*. He has the bottle in his bag, and he'd like the brother to smell it again, in front of the lady.

"I don't need to smell it, young man. I made it." Aldane doesn't take his eyes off the wax. "Foxglove. Steeped, strained, measured into a dark glass with our mark tied round the neck so nobody mistakes it for cordial. Jassan had it from me since midwinter. Six drops in water of a night, for a heart that ran too fast and then too slow." He shifts his weight onto the stick. "That is what you smelled, sister. Bruised green, gone bitter. It's the smell of a remedy."

He answers the question Sefa actually asked, slowly, one piece at a time. "Why was I sure? I wasn't sure in the way you mean. He was lying across the stand with his hand in the spill and his face the colour such men's faces go. He was a man I'd been dosing for a weak heart, and his heart stopped. I've seen that more times than I have teeth left." Then he says the other half. "Foxglove is also what stops a heart when there's too much of it. Six drops mend. Sixty kill. A third of the bottle was left, and I filled it on the tenth day before." He lets that stand without making more of it. "That's arithmetic, not an accusation. I said heart because it was the likelier answer, and because the woman on the stair had found one dead man that morning already."

Sefa asks about the seal. Aldane leans closer to the bead than his back really allows.

"No hammer. You're right. It isn't the Just God's." He breathes out through his nose. "Scales for trade. The eye shut means the word is sealed and not to be read. That's Waukeen's mark, the Merchant's Friend, and old. Her bond-clerks in the Gate pressed it into lead, before she went silent in my grandfather's time. Nobody in Beregost presses that. Nobody has pressed it anywhere for a long while, as far as I know. I've seen it once, on a bond in our own coffer that came down from the Gate before I took vows." His finger hovers over the wax and doesn't touch it. "The old clerks used to say a sealed word knew whose hands opened it. Clerks say a great many things."

He straightens with a small grunt and looks at the box, not at any of them.

"He came up the hill the day before he died. Not for drops. He had plenty left." The stick shifts on the flags. "He sat on that bench where you're sitting and asked me whether a man is guilty for what he writes down for others. Whether the pen answers for the hand that pays it." Aldane is quiet for a moment. "I told him it depends what he does with what he knows once he's written it. He thanked me and went down the hill. I've been wondering since what he chose."

In the passage behind them the basin brother has stopped with his basin half-raised and is listening. The girl with the baby shifts it to her other hip. Out in the forecourt the fountain chuckles. Up on the steps Coll still has his face tipped to the sun and his eyes shut. Thirty feet along the inside of the wall, the man with the straw has turned it round to the other side of his mouth. Above them all, the bell rope hangs still.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Pell Dunmore: Pell doesn't get up. He keeps the oak square on his knees and his hands on the handles, and watches the old man come down the passage — not the stick, not the bald head, but the eyes, and where they stop. They stopped on the box before they stopped on the novice from the Gate. He files that.

Low, to Bram, without turning his head: "The straw's Coll's after all. Two fingers off the knee and the man moved. So Thale's got three on us, not two, and he lets us count wrong on purpose. Mind that when you talk prices."

Then to Odda, quiet, neighbour to neighbour, his eyes still on the passage: "Mistress Brand. One thing, and I'm not Vell's and I'm not the Fist. The paper Harl signed in the spring — did you see it? Was there wax on it, and under the wax a little grey disc of lead? Round mark, scales, an eye shut?" He waits for her face more than her words. "And Dobbin's wagons — did Dobbin borrow from Vell too, or only your Harl? Because if every driver who went past the Lionsfang ford this year had Vell's paper on his house first, then the road didn't eat them. The ledger did."

He lets Sefa take Brother Aldane; it's her ground and her beads. But as the old man draws level with the bench, Pell shifts the box an inch so the green bead on the hasp catches the light from the door — nothing pointed, a porter easing a weight — and says, mild, looking up: "Brother. You knew Jassan Ferr by sight, Mistress Pike says. You picked up his bottle, smelled it, and said *heart*." A beat, no edge in it. "I've got the bottle in my bag. I'd like you to smell it again. In front of the lady."

Bram Halloway: “I’m sorry, Odda. No bodies is a hard way to be told you’re a widow.”

I read Jassan’s note once more, then offer it back. “May Sefa and Pell read this too? It ties Harl’s loss to the missing wagons we’ve just heard about.”

I keep my voice low. “Did Harl pledge the house when he borrowed, or is that what Vell told you afterward? And did Jassan ever explain what he meant by ‘done enough with my pen’?”

To Pell, quietly: “Same ford. Same Dobbin at the Juggler. That part of Coll’s story holds.”

I make room for the old brother to reach Sefa, keeping Pell and the box close. “I have twenty-two gold to put toward buying the note. Before I ask either of you for the rest, let’s hear what Brother Aldane knows.”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa steps aside from the doorway so the old brother can pass, and bows her head a little—not a temple bow, but the nod of one who once wore the same kind of saffron work. "Brother Aldane. I'm Sefa Marrin. I used to keep a ward in the Lower City, so I know the smell of a still-room and the sound of a man being too polite about his knees. Thank you for coming out."

She walks with him as far as Pell's bench, close enough that all three of them can speak low and still keep the box in view. "We won't keep you long. Three days ago you were called down to the Coast Way for Jassan Ferr. I'd like to hear, plainly, what you found that made you say *heart* so certain. And this—" She turns to Pell, indicating the satchel. "The little brown vial with your house's half-sun. Was that something made here, and what would it be? It has a bitter green smell, like stems left too long in water. A man with a weak heart might take such a thing. Or be given it."

She folds her hands again. "There's a second matter, if you know it. The box carries a lead seal under green wax: scales and a shut eye, but no hammer. That isn't Tyr's stamp. You've served this town through too many quarrels not to know who presses a private seal like that in Beregost."

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I return Jassan’s letter to Odda. “You’re right. Missing isn’t dead. I’m sorry.”

To Aldane I say, “Thank you for telling us what you know—and what you don’t. Did Jassan mention anyone he meant to take his knowledge to?”

Then I turn to Sefa and Pell, keeping my voice low.

“We can’t settle the missing wagons before noon. We can get Odda’s house clear of this. Will you lend me eighteen gold between you, against my share of the fee? I’ll put in twenty-two. No payment unless Vell produces Harl’s original note and gives a written release of the house with it.”

I glance toward the forecourt. “I don’t favour splitting up with those three watching. We could go together, keep the box in our custody until the purchase is finished, then take Jassan’s warning to Cowl. Before Vell gets the books, not after.”

I wait for their answer rather than reaching for anyone’s purse.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa glances once toward the passage where the basin brother is listening, then back to Aldane. She lets the hush settle.

"You've told us what the bottle held and what it could do. One thing more, Brother, and I'll stop troubling you." She keeps her hands folded over her beads. "Would foxglove kill a man as he slept? Would it be quick, or would he know—wake, fall, break the stand, lie with his hand in the spill? And the half-sun tag tied on the neck: could a stranger have slipped that from the temple's own shelves, or would it have to pass through hands like yours?"

She pauses, then says, more softly, "Also: the old bond seal from Waukeen's clerks. If a man came to you asking what it meant—or where to buy its silence for a box of ledgers—what would you have told him? You've already stood once at the edge of what he chose."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell sits with that a moment. The passage is cool against his back and the box is warm on his knees, and he finds he's been holding it a little tighter since *foxglove*.

"Arithmetic." He says it to the old man, not unkindly. "Then do me one more sum, Brother, since you filled it. Ten nights at six drops — how much ought to have been gone? And how much *was*?" He watches the knuckled hand, not the face. "Because there's two ways a man ends with his hand in sixty drops of his own medicine. Somebody pours it for him. Or he sits on this bench, asks you whether a pen answers for the hand that pays it, goes home, seals his master's books with a mark nobody in Beregost can press, writes to the Fist, burns the letter because he thinks it isn't enough — and pours it himself." His voice has gone quiet. "I'd like to know which, before I walk this up to Vell's counter and let him tell the town it was *heart*."

Then, to Sefa and Bram, still low, the plan coming together as he speaks it: "Here's where I've got to. Waukeen's bond-seal, from the Gate, that nobody here owns. Jassan didn't buy that at a Beregost notary — he got it from somewhere Vell keeps old paper, or he brought it down from the Gate himself. Either way he meant it to be opened by someone who'd *ask* why it was there. That's not Vell. That's not Thale either; Thale wants to read it and sell it." He nods toward the hill, where the market lies. "That's Cowl. A loud red-faced man who collects talk about the Way and gets paid for none of it. The trooper said tell him anyway."

"So: I keep my word. The box goes to Vell before nightfall, unopened, seal whole — I said I would and I will. But it goes to his counter with Sergeant Cowl standing beside me and Mistress Brand behind him, and Vell can break Waukeen's lead with the Fist watching, or explain to the Fist why he'd rather not. That's not selling it and it's not stealing it. That's delivering it in daylight." He glances at Odda. "And Bram — don't buy her note yet. If Vell's book shows what I think it shows, that note's not worth forty. It's not worth four. Buying it is paying him for the rope."

He lifts the box off his knees and stands. "Noon muster's in under two hours. We go to the market post now, all three, box in the middle, straight across the forecourt past our friend on the steps — and I tell Coll to his face where we're going, because a man who's hired to watch should have something honest to report for once. Brother — one last thing. If a bond under Waukeen's seal came down from the Gate to your coffer before you took vows, whose name was on it?"

scenes.narration:
Bram folds Jassan's letter along its creases and gives it back to Odda. She takes it at once and puts it away inside her shawl, against her ribs. When he says missing isn't dead, she looks at him a moment longer than she has looked at anyone this morning.

"No. It isn't." That's all she says about it.

Brother Aldane hears Bram's thanks with a small dip of his head. When Bram asks whether Jassan named anyone he meant to take what he knew to, the old man takes his time.

"No name, sir. He asked me something else on his way out, though. Whether this house keeps papers for people who aren't brothers." His thumb moves on the head of the stick. "I told him the coffer is for the temple's own bonds and nobody else's. He nodded, as if he'd expected me to say so. And he left a tithe in the box by the door. More than a clerk's." He stops there, as though he'd thought about saying more and decided against it.

Bram turns to the other two and keeps his voice low. He asks for eighteen gold between them against his share of the fee, puts his own twenty-two beside it, and sets his conditions: nothing gets paid unless Vell produces Harl's own note and writes out a release of the house to go with it. He wants all of them going together with the box in their keeping, and Cowl told before Vell has the books. Then he leaves the purses alone. Odda hears the conditions from an arm's length away.

"Harl's note in my hand, and the house written free." She says it under her breath, as if checking a sum. "That's how it should have been done in the spring."

Sefa looks once down the passage at the basin brother, then puts her questions. Aldane answers them in the order she asked, the way he would read off a list of doses.

"Asleep? No. Too much foxglove isn't quiet, sister. The stomach goes first. A man is sick, and sick again. Then he sees yellow, and rings round the candle flame, and his heart stumbles. It takes hours, and he knows about all of them." He looks at the flags. "Mistress Pike sent for me before she'd touched anything. The bed was clean. There was no basin and no mess on him or the floor, only the spill under his hand. A heart that stops by itself stops quickly. That's what I saw. What happened before the stand went over, I didn't see."

"The tags are mine. I tie every one in the still-room, and no stranger climbs my stair without my knees hearing him coming." The corner of his mouth moves. "But the tag goes on the glass. It doesn't go in the drops. Once a bottle has gone out of this door, anyone can pour anything into it."

On the seal he shakes his head. "Nobody asked me. Not Jassan, not anyone, until you did this morning. And if a man had come up the hill wanting to buy that seal's silence, I'd have sent him back down. We don't keep it in the still-room."

Pell has the box warm on his knees and the cool wall at his back, and he asks for the sum. The old man's hand stays steady on the stick while he works it out aloud.

"Six drops a night for ten nights is sixty. The glass holds near two hundred. So two thirds should be left, and a third is. That's sixty drops more than his dose, gone somewhere." He lets that sit. "The stain by the stand is a palm across and soaked into the grain. Sixty drops spilled on a board would make about that much. I'd guess that's where most of it went. I'd guess. I didn't measure the floor." He doesn't say which of Pell's two roads it was. He doesn't seem to think he knows.

Pell gives the other two his reckoning, low and fast: Waukeen's seal meant for someone who would ask why it was there, the box delivered at dusk with the seal whole and Sergeant Cowl standing beside it, and Bram not to buy the note, because if the books show what he thinks they show, paying the forty is paying Vell for the rope.

Odda hears that too. She doesn't raise her voice.

"Worth forty or worth four, it's Vell's paper with Harl's mark on it and my house in it." She looks at Pell straight, the way she'd look at a carter quoting a bad price. "If the Fist reads his books, the Fist takes a season about it. Vell calls the debt the day after the box goes back. Jassan said so. I've been to the Fist once already this year, and they wrote my husband down."

Pell lifts the box off his knees and stands up with it. His last question is about the bond that came down from the Gate to the temple's coffer, and whose name was on it. Aldane frowns, the way the very old frown when a drawer in their memory sticks.

"A glazier's, I think. Something for the east window. The parties' names I've lost." He taps the stick once. "I remember the clerk's name was written larger than theirs, under the seal. Her bond-clerks were proud. Which clerk, I couldn't tell you this morning. The coffer is the Revered Brother's key, not mine. After the noon prayers I could ask him to let me look. My knees will want the whole hour for that stair, mind."

Behind him the basin brother has given up pretending to work and simply stands there holding the basin. The carter with the bandaged hand clears his throat at the end of the line, and the brother moves on to him.

Out on the steps, Coll opens his eyes. He doesn't sit up. He just turns his head on the pillar's base until he can see the side door and the thin man standing in it with the oak box held square. Thirty feet along the forecourt wall, the man with the straw takes it out of his mouth. The fountain goes on chuckling, and the bell rope hangs still in its tower.
