messages.text:
Pell leans an elbow on the counter, not quite touching the clerk's tidy desk, and takes Vell in the way he'd take in a lock — unhurried.

"A few things, Master Vell, since it's our necks on the Coast Way and not yours." He counts them off on his fingers, mirroring Vell's tapping. "One: what does this box look like? Size, iron or wood, whose seal is on it — yours or Ferr's? I'd hate to carry home the wrong one. Two: who holds the key to that room now? The cooper, a landlady, the Fist? If the door's locked and the owner's absent, I'll want to know whether I'm *allowed* in or merely *expected* to be." He lets that sit a heartbeat. "Three: who else knows the box is there and wants it? A man doesn't pay seventy-five gold for a stroll down the road to fetch a parcel. And four—" his voice drops a little, "how did Jassan Ferr die? Fever, drink, or did somebody help him along? It matters to how carefully I open his door."

He glances sideways at Sefa and Bram, then back. "Answer straight and we're gone inside the quarter-hour."
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

Pell straightens off the counter. He's got what the lock will give him; forcing it further only scratches the plate.

"Oak, iron corners, brass with your name, red wax, key between O and V. Seal whole." He says it back flat, a runner repeating an address. "One more, and then we're gone. Gerrit Thale — does he send men, or does he send coin? A man who sends coin, I'd like to know whether Wenna Pike has had a visitor since the brother from the Song went home." He nods at the sealed note. "If she says no, good. If she says yes, that tells us whether we're walking to a parcel or to an empty room, and I'd rather know on the Coast Way than on your counter at dusk with nothing in our hands."

He doesn't wait long for the answer — he's already turning to the other two, voice lower. "Walk in by the front with the note, Bram, you've got the face for honest errands. Sefa with you; a landlady who's had a death in the house will talk to a woman with beads before she talks to either of us. I'll come in behind and have a look at the room before anyone's hands are on anything — a man's room tells you how he died quicker than a brother from a temple does. And I'll want a look at the back of the cooper's yard. Three days is a long time for a locked box to sit unmolested in a town where everyone knows the clerk's dead."

He gives Vell a short, civil nod. "Before nightfall, Master Vell."

Pell stops at the gatepost as if to shift his pack, and his thumb finds the chalk mark without looking at it. Circle, stroke through. He's drawn that one himself, on the Wide, more than once. Someone from home has been here, or someone taught by someone from home.

He doesn't rub it out. A rubbed mark tells the chalker someone read it.

He closes the two paces to Bram and Sefa, falling in at Bram's shield shoulder so his mouth is near Bram's ear and his back is to the street. Low, conversational, like a man remarking on the weather: "Gatepost. Chalk. That's a Guild mark, or a good copy — it means *this house is watched, keep clear or report.* Fresh since the last rain. So Thale's man, or somebody else's, has been standing on this street in the last day, and may still be." He lets his eyes drift, not his head: the yards opposite, the lodging-house windows, the lane ends. "Don't look round. Go up with the note like honest folk. Talk to Wenna on the gallery where I can see you, and don't let her open that middle door until I've come up the back — if the shutter's closed but the room's been visited, I want to see the sill before three pairs of boots are on it."

To Sefa, a touch softer: "Ask her if anyone's come asking after Jassan's things. A friend, a cousin, a man with a Gate voice. Watch her hands when she answers, not her face."

Then he peels off, unhurried, as if he's just the third hireling who'd rather have a word with the cooper than climb stairs. He gives the man in the leather sleeves a nod and a "Morning," and walks along the stacked staves toward the back of the yard — looking for the rear of the building under the middle shutter, any lane behind, a drainpipe or the beam-ends he can go up by, and above all for anyone who has the gate in view and no barrel in front of them.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

Pell comes back up the yard at an easy walk, hands where she can see them, and stops a little short of the stair so he's not crowding her — but close enough to read her hands when she answers.

"Fair's fair, Mistress Pike. A room's a room and a dead man's rent doesn't pay itself." He glances at Bram. "Three and four. We can settle that out of the fee and take it off the top before Vell counts his shares — he'd rather pay rent than argue with a landlady, and if he'd rather argue, that's his quarrel with her, not ours." He's already fishing the purse out, slow, letting the coin be seen. "I'll put it in your hand myself if it saves a walk."

Then, lighter, as if it's an afterthought: "You said *him*. Who came asking before us? Broad fellow, quiet, talks like the Gate? And what did he offer — the rent, or more than the rent?" He nods up at the gallery without looking away from her. "And that padlock's new since the brother went home. Yours? Or did somebody put it on and give you the key?"

He keeps the purse open but not yet paying — the coin is for after she's answered.

Pell slides the purse back into his coat without a word about it. She's right; a landlady who won't be paid twice is a landlady he'd trust further than most.

"Open it, Mistress Pike. Then let me go in first and alone for the length of a breath or two before the chain mail follows — not because I doubt you, but because a floor tells you things before it's been walked on." He says it mild, a craftsman asking for room at the bench. "Bram, Sefa — stay on the gallery with her a moment. And one of you keep an eye down the Way. Our broad friend was on the awning post when we came in and he's walking off toward town now, no faster than anyone else. That's a man going to tell somebody we're here, not a man giving up. He said this afternoon. I'd believe him."

He waits for the padlock to come off, then before he steps over the threshold he crouches at the door and looks: the sill, the dust on the boards, whether the window shutter's latch sits as she left it, the bed stripped as she said, and — most of all — whether there's a forearm's length of oak with iron corners anywhere in sight, and whether the wax on it is red, whole, and pressed only once.

Over his shoulder, quietly, to Wenna, not accusing, almost kind: "You went in once. Stripped the bed, opened the window. Was there anything else in the room that morning that isn't in it now? A paper, a purse, a letter with a name on it? I'm not Vell and I'm not the Fist. I'd just rather hear it from you up here than find out from Thale's man this afternoon."
[Roll the die]
[Request an allowed reroll — Investigation: reading the dust and floorboards of Jassan's room from the doorway, before anyone walks on them]
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

Pell doesn't step in yet. He stays crouched on the sill a heartbeat longer, then speaks without turning, low enough that it's for the gallery and not the yard.

"Box is here. On the table, square to the edge, like he left it to go to bed." A pause. "Wax on the hasp is whole. And it's green. Round seal. Vell's is red and square." He lets that land. "So either Vell sealed it with a ring he didn't show us, or somebody else sealed Jassan Ferr's box before Jassan Ferr stopped breathing — and whoever it was, it wasn't done in a hurry. That's a fat, careful bead."

Then he stands and goes in — along the wall where the dust is already disturbed by Wenna's shoes, not across the swept middle — and goes first not to the box but to the nightstand. He doesn't touch the vial. He bends and smells it, and the stain, and looks at the stopper: wax, cork, whether it's been drawn and put back. "Mistress Pike. This vial. Was it here the morning you found him? And the stain — was that wet?" He keeps his voice level. "The brother said heart. Did the brother see this?"

He crosses to the grate, crouches, and with the tip of a dagger — not his fingers — eases the twist of paper off the ash onto the hearthstone so the unburnt end can be read without crumbling the black end. "Sefa, you read a clerk's hand better than I do. Come in along the wall, where her tracks are. Don't cross the middle yet. There's a half-burnt paper here I'd like two pairs of eyes on." Then to Bram, still at the door: "Keep the stair. If our broad friend's gone to fetch coin or company, we've got less of the morning than we thought. And Bram — nobody touches that wax. Not us, not her, not Vell till he's standing over it saying out loud it isn't his."

Last, he glances at the back shutter's latch from where he kneels — checking it's seated the way a woman would leave it after closing a window for the smell, and not the way a man would leave it after coming in by the lean-to roof.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

Pell looks at the scrap a long moment. Then he takes the receipt-leaf's twin — a blank page torn from the back of his own little ration tally in the pack — folds the brown curl inside it flat, and tucks it into the inner pocket of his coat where the purse was. He does it slowly, so Wenna on the sill can see what he's taking and that it isn't hers.

"Mistress Pike. This was in his grate. A letter he started and burnt. It's addressed to a sergeant of the Fist. Does the name Cowl mean anything to you? Did Jassan ever have a trooper up here, or go down to the Fist's post in town?"

He stands and comes back along the wall to the doorway, and speaks for the gallery only, flat and quick. "Three things, and none of them are heart. One: the seal on that box is green and round, and Vell told us red and square — so either he lied about his own ring or somebody else had a key to this room and time to melt wax in it. Two: the vial on the stand has a little half-sun inked on the tag. That's Lathander's mark. That's the Song of the Morning's mark. And the brother from the Song picked it up, smelled it, set it down and said *heart*. Three—" he taps his coat where the scrap is, "Jassan Ferr was writing to a Sergeant Cowl of the Fist. All that's left of it says *the notes were sold before*. A clerk's phrase. A moneylender sells a man's debt to one buyer, then sells the same paper to another — and the ledgers in that box are the only place it'd show." He looks at Bram. "That's why the fee's seventy-five and not fifteen. That's why Thale wants it, and that's why Vell talks about the wax like it's his neck."

He breathes out. "I'm a hireling. I take the box to the man who hired me — that's the job and I'll do it. But I'm not carrying it down that stair with a seal on it that isn't his and letting him tell me afterwards I broke it. Sefa — can you make a fair copy of that seal's shape, or press it in a bit of candle-wax from the nightstand so we've a record of it whole before it leaves this room? And I want that vial wrapped and in my satchel, stopper in, tag on. If a brother of the Song called it heart, a *different* brother of the Song can tell us what it actually is, this afternoon, before Thale's man comes back to ask Wenna again."

Then, quieter, to Wenna, not pressing: "The empty peg. Was it a coat? I only ask because if Jassan Ferr went to the Fist's post, he went wearing it, and a sergeant might remember the coat before he remembers the man."

Pell nods at Wenna — *the coat, owed, fine* — and leaves it there. A landlady who gives back a gold piece she could have kept has told him all he needs about what she took and why.

He kneels at the grate again and picks up a stick of cold charcoal, the black end of a burnt splint. "Sefa, give me your light on the hasp a moment." He tears a second blank leaf from his ration tally, lays it flat over the green bead, and rubs the charcoal across it light and even, the way a boy takes a brass off a tomb — the round mark, its device, the edge of the bead, the join where wax meets iron. He lifts it off without the paper touching anything but wax, checks it against the light, and holds it so Bram can set Vell's red square beside it. "There. Round. Not his. Dated by the bell, witnessed by three and Wenna Pike's own eyes. If Vell says we broke it, that's what I lay on his counter." He folds it in with the letter.

Then the vial: he takes the cloth that wraps his rations, winds it round the dark glass with the tag still on and the cork still in, and settles it upright in the healer's satchel between two potions where it won't roll. "That's ours. Not Vell's."

Only now does he go to the table and put both hands on the drop handles. He lifts the box an inch, feels the weight shift, tilts it a hair and listens — whether something slides inside like bound books, or whether it's lighter than seventy-five gold has any right to be. He sets it down again. "Right. It goes down the stair with me carrying and Bram's shield in front. Nobody sets it on the ground between here and the counting-house." He looks at the other two. "But the Song's on the way up the hill, more or less, and the bell says we've the whole of the day. I'd like Sefa to put her head in and ask for Brother Aldane — a novice of the hospice asking a brother about a sick man's medicine is the most natural thing in Faerûn. Ten minutes. I'll stand in the porch with the box in my arms and Bram at my shoulder, and if the old man says *heart* twice, I'll want to see his face when he says it."

He turns to Wenna last, civil. "Thale's man comes back this afternoon. When he does, tell him the truth — Vell's hirelings took it on Vell's paper, and you've the receipt. Don't tell him which way we went." He pauses on the sill. "And Mistress Pike — if a red-faced sergeant ever does come up your stair asking after Jassan Ferr's letters, there's one he didn't finish. I've got it. He can find me through Vell's counter, or he can find me not at all."

He hefts the box and waits for Bram to take the stair first.
[Roll the die]
[Request an allowed reroll — Sleight of Hand: a light charcoal rubbing of the seal over sun-warmed wax, taking its mark without smearing it]
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

Pell stands in the doorway with the weight of it against his chest and looks at the rubbing once more before he folds it away for good.

"Scales and a shut eye, on lead under the wax. That's a bond seal, the kind a notary puts on a thing he wants to outlast the paper inside it — and scales with a blind eye is the Blind God's mark. Tyr's house, or someone borrowing it." He says it slow. "Jassan Ferr didn't lock up his master's books. He had them *witnessed*. He made evidence, and then he wrote to the Fist, and then his heart stopped. And now the man whose books they are wants them back with the seal he *didn't* put on them still whole, so he can say nobody read them." A short breath. "I've carried worse for worse men. But I'll say it once so it's said: I don't like this box."

He turns to Bram, low. "The back's a lean-to roof and a nettle lane with a ditch. Good for me alone with empty hands. No good for chain mail, and no good for this — I'm not dropping seventy-five gold of somebody's ruin into a ditch. We go out the front, all three, box in the middle, straight up the smith street in the sun. Nobody robs three armed people between a Fist trooper and forty hammers at midmorning. The two at the corner want to see which way we turn, not to take it. Let them see."

"But Vell said *before nightfall*, not *before noon*. So here's the day." He nods up the hill. "The Song first. A temple's a safe place to set a box down — nobody's robbing Lathander's porch — and Sefa asks for Brother Aldane and what a half-sun vial of green bitter is for. While she does, Bram, you go to Vell's counter without us and without the box, and you buy Odda Brand's note *now*, while he still needs you. He'll sell it cheap to a man who's holding his box. Don't tell him where it is. Tell him it's safe and coming at dusk, and that his wax is whole." A thin smile. "Which is true. It's just not his wax."

"And the letter to Cowl?" He pats his coat. "That doesn't go to Vell. Ever. We decide between us by dusk whether it goes to the sergeant. Agreed? Then Bram takes the stair first."

Pell doesn't move off the sill, but his voice comes down the stair before Bram's can, easy and loud enough for the yard — the voice of a hireling with nothing on his mind.

"Boy. The big man's heard you. Tell Mistress Brand *yes, before noon, at the Song.* Nothing else — not the counting-house, not a number. You've said forty once in a cooper's yard already and that's once too often." He shifts the box onto one hip just long enough to fish a copper out and flip it down the stair to him. "That's for the running. Go the long way round the smith street. There's a man walking up it ahead of you and I'd rather he didn't hear what you're carrying."

Then, low, to the other two on the gallery, his back to the lane: "Change of plan, and a small one. That boy just told half the Coast Way that Bram's got business at Vell's counter about forty gold, and the one by the wall took a good look at this box and walked off toward town the moment he heard it. So Bram doesn't go to Vell's alone — not now, not with Thale's man knowing his name and his errand. We all go up to the Song. Odda's at the almshouse door till the noon bell; Bram talks to her there with his own ears, Sefa asks for Brother Aldane, and I sit in the porch with Lathander's doorkeeper and this on my knees. Vell gets his box at dusk like he said. He doesn't get it a minute sooner."

He glances at Sefa. "And you're right about the hammer. I jumped. Scales with no hammer and a shut eye — that's not Tyr's house, that's somebody who wanted it to *look* like a court's seal to anyone who didn't grow up next to a temple. Which means Jassan didn't go to a notary. He went to somebody private. The old brother might know who stamps lead in this town."

Last, to Wenna, as he steps onto the gallery and makes room for Bram to take the stair: "One outline in the dust, Mistress Pike. He set it down once and never lifted it again. You told it true." A nod. "If anyone with Gate shoulders asks, we went up the hill. Everyone goes up the hill."

He waits for Bram's shield to be one step below him, then follows, the box held square and both hands on the handles, Sefa behind with her light put away.

Pell doesn't break stride and doesn't shift the box. His grip stays on the drop handles; his eyes stay on the broad man's hands, not his face.

Low, for Bram and Sefa only: "Don't stop and don't speed up. Bram, shield-side to him and half a pace ahead of me. Sefa, my other side. We walk straight at the trooper in the doorway like he's an old friend — I want this said within ten feet of a Fist uniform, not twenty." A beat. "If he wants to talk, let me. He's Gate. I know what that sounds like."

When the broad man comes level — or stops in front of them — Pell gives him the kind of nod one Lower City man gives another on a strange street: neither friendly nor not. And as his left hand resettles on the handle, two fingers tap the iron corner in a small, plain rhythm — the Cant's shrug: *hired, not freelancing, nothing here's yours.* He watches whether the man's eyes flick to it.

Aloud, pitched easy, Gate vowels coming back into it without effort: "Morning. You'll be Coll. Thale's man." Civil. "You've got your master's coin and I've got mine. Box goes to the name on the brass. Thale wants to read Vell's books, he can go to Vell's counter and bid like a gentleman, or he can wait for the Fist to want to read them, which—" a glance at the trooper's doorway, not hidden, "—from the look of things is going to happen sooner than he'd like. Either way it's not a street matter. Not in the smiths' street at midmorning with Lathander's bell going." He lets a half-step go by. "I'd put it to him that way. You've been paid to carry a box, not to start a thing. So have I."

He keeps walking toward the doorway and the trooper's knife, and doesn't look back for the man with the straw. Bram can tell him if the straw moves.

Pell keeps walking. The box doesn't shift.

To Coll, over his shoulder, same street voice: "Eighty's a good number for a thing that isn't mine to sell. Tell your master I heard it. And I heard *Nashkel.*" A nod, nothing more. "Temple steps. In the sun."

Then, low, to the other two as the smithy falls behind: "Well. That's three parties who want this box and two of them say the wax isn't Vell's. Thale's man just told us Vell's debtors go down the Way to Nashkel and don't come back — and the Fist's got caravans vanishing between Beregost and Nashkel that nobody can account for. If that's one story and not two, then Jassan wasn't writing to Cowl about double-sold paper. He was writing about *men.*" He breathes out through his nose. "I still don't sell what I was hired to carry. Not for eighty, not on the street. But I'm no longer sure the man I carry it *to* gets to open it alone behind his counter either."

He glances at Sefa. "That was well done, the shouting. Loud is safe. I'd forgotten." A flicker of a smile. "Don't make a habit of it around me."

They reach the trooper's doorway. Pell slows there — doesn't stop, just lets the box rest on his hip a moment, as a tired porter might — and speaks to the Fist man as to a neighbour, Gate vowels still in his mouth. "Morning. Your sergeant — Cowl, is it? Red face, loud? Where's he found at this hour?" He nods back down the hill, where Coll leans on nothing and the straw-man has stopped again. "Only there's a dead clerk's box here that three different people have a price for, and I'd as soon the Fist knew where it slept tonight before somebody decides it shouldn't."

He doesn't wait long for an answer; he hefts the box and heads on for the turn to the Song, Bram's shield between him and the street.

Pell takes the forecourt in the way he took the street: fountain, two novices, the queue, the side passage, Coll three steps up with his legs out, the straw-man finding his wall. Then he picks his ground.

Not the steps. Coll chose the steps; Pell won't share them with a man who wants his box. He goes instead to the side door, to the end of the ragged line, and finds the brother with the basin when he comes near.

"Brother. Three of us, on an errand that's turned heavier than it was at breakfast." He lifts the box an inch to show it. "A dead man's strongbox, sealed, that I'm sworn to carry unopened to the man it belongs to at dusk. Between now and then there's two men on your steps and one on your gate who'd like to carry it elsewhere. I'd ask leave to sit inside your door with it on my knees — the passage, the porch, wherever your doorkeeper can see me and the god can too. I'll touch nothing and I'll bother no one. The lady's a hospice novice from the Gate; she'll want a word with Brother Aldane, about Jassan Ferr's medicine — he knew the man. The big one has business with the woman in the grey shawl, and she's come a long way to say it." He adds a silver to the basin, not making a show of it. "For the fountain lye, since they're arguing over it."

To Bram and Sefa, low, before they part: "I'll be in that doorway with the box in sight of both of you. Bram — hear Odda out, but don't put coin in anyone's hand until the three of us have talked. If she says Jassan told her the debt would be called *once the box came back*, ask her what he said would happen if it didn't. Sefa — the vial, the half-sun tag, and one thing more: ask the old brother who in Beregost stamps lead under wax. Scales and a shut eye. A town this size has one man who does that, and a temple knows who."

Then, as he settles on the bench inside the door with the oak square on his knees and his back to the whitewash, he looks out through the opening at Coll on the steps, and raises his chin a quarter inch — *I see you; I'm not coming over.* He lets Coll stew in the sun a while. A man who's been paid to wait can wait.

And he watches the straw-man at the gate, because the straw-man isn't Coll's. Coll came with one friend, both times. The straw-man was at the corner before any of them, and he's the only one who hasn't been introduced.

Pell doesn't get up. He keeps the oak square on his knees and his hands on the handles, and watches the old man come down the passage — not the stick, not the bald head, but the eyes, and where they stop. They stopped on the box before they stopped on the novice from the Gate. He files that.

Low, to Bram, without turning his head: "The straw's Coll's after all. Two fingers off the knee and the man moved. So Thale's got three on us, not two, and he lets us count wrong on purpose. Mind that when you talk prices."

Then to Odda, quiet, neighbour to neighbour, his eyes still on the passage: "Mistress Brand. One thing, and I'm not Vell's and I'm not the Fist. The paper Harl signed in the spring — did you see it? Was there wax on it, and under the wax a little grey disc of lead? Round mark, scales, an eye shut?" He waits for her face more than her words. "And Dobbin's wagons — did Dobbin borrow from Vell too, or only your Harl? Because if every driver who went past the Lionsfang ford this year had Vell's paper on his house first, then the road didn't eat them. The ledger did."

He lets Sefa take Brother Aldane; it's her ground and her beads. But as the old man draws level with the bench, Pell shifts the box an inch so the green bead on the hasp catches the light from the door — nothing pointed, a porter easing a weight — and says, mild, looking up: "Brother. You knew Jassan Ferr by sight, Mistress Pike says. You picked up his bottle, smelled it, and said *heart*." A beat, no edge in it. "I've got the bottle in my bag. I'd like you to smell it again. In front of the lady."

Pell sits with that a moment. The passage is cool against his back and the box is warm on his knees, and he finds he's been holding it a little tighter since *foxglove*.

"Arithmetic." He says it to the old man, not unkindly. "Then do me one more sum, Brother, since you filled it. Ten nights at six drops — how much ought to have been gone? And how much *was*?" He watches the knuckled hand, not the face. "Because there's two ways a man ends with his hand in sixty drops of his own medicine. Somebody pours it for him. Or he sits on this bench, asks you whether a pen answers for the hand that pays it, goes home, seals his master's books with a mark nobody in Beregost can press, writes to the Fist, burns the letter because he thinks it isn't enough — and pours it himself." His voice has gone quiet. "I'd like to know which, before I walk this up to Vell's counter and let him tell the town it was *heart*."

Then, to Sefa and Bram, still low, the plan coming together as he speaks it: "Here's where I've got to. Waukeen's bond-seal, from the Gate, that nobody here owns. Jassan didn't buy that at a Beregost notary — he got it from somewhere Vell keeps old paper, or he brought it down from the Gate himself. Either way he meant it to be opened by someone who'd *ask* why it was there. That's not Vell. That's not Thale either; Thale wants to read it and sell it." He nods toward the hill, where the market lies. "That's Cowl. A loud red-faced man who collects talk about the Way and gets paid for none of it. The trooper said tell him anyway."

"So: I keep my word. The box goes to Vell before nightfall, unopened, seal whole — I said I would and I will. But it goes to his counter with Sergeant Cowl standing beside me and Mistress Brand behind him, and Vell can break Waukeen's lead with the Fist watching, or explain to the Fist why he'd rather not. That's not selling it and it's not stealing it. That's delivering it in daylight." He glances at Odda. "And Bram — don't buy her note yet. If Vell's book shows what I think it shows, that note's not worth forty. It's not worth four. Buying it is paying him for the rope."

He lifts the box off his knees and stands. "Noon muster's in under two hours. We go to the market post now, all three, box in the middle, straight across the forecourt past our friend on the steps — and I tell Coll to his face where we're going, because a man who's hired to watch should have something honest to report for once. Brother — one last thing. If a bond under Waukeen's seal came down from the Gate to your coffer before you took vows, whose name was on it?"

Good table. Genuinely.

What worked: the world kept its own clock. Vell's counter, Wenna's rent book, Tobin's hammer, Coll leaning on a pillar like he'd been there an hour — nothing waited for us, and nobody handed us anything. Wenna giving back the gold piece and refusing to say where the coat went told me more about her than a page of exposition would have. Aldane's "that's arithmetic, not an accusation" was the line of the session. And the mystery escalated honestly — foxglove, Waukeen's lead, the Nashkel drivers — each piece earned, none of it dropped on us.

What I'd watch: the dice were brutal on me and the session leaned investigative, so Pell spent a lot of rounds failing to read dust and charcoal while the plot moved on through NPC dialogue. That's partly the dice and partly my own choices — I kept rolling for things the room was going to tell us anyway. A couple of those checks might have been better as "you simply see it." Also, the later narration summarised the other two players' actions at length before mine; it sometimes felt like reading a transcript rather than being in the scene.

Small thing: the session ended on a strong beat — three of us at the door, Coll's head turning, the straw coming out of the man's mouth — but it ended without a wrap. A sentence of "where things stand" would have landed it.

The cast is excellent. Odda in particular — "widow is the Fist's word, not mine." I'd come back for the market post and Cowl.

A few things.

The back way. I scouted the lean-to roof and the nettle lane in round 3 and then never used them. Pell is a roof-runner; that's the whole character. By the time we had the box, I'd talked myself out of it for sound reasons — chain mail, a dead man's ledgers in a ditch — but I half wish I'd sent Bram and Sefa out the front with the empty-handed look and gone over the shed myself with the box roped to my back. It would have been riskier and more *Pell*. Instead I spent the session being the cautious one, which is a fine role but not the one on the sheet.

The straw-man. I clocked him as the odd one out and wanted to peel off and shadow *him* — see where he went when he thought nobody was looking, who he reported to. Coll was theatre; the straw was the real tail. But leaving the box meant leaving the box, and I'd just made a speech about not setting it down. Fair enough. Still itches.

Wenna. I let the coat go because I liked her, and I think that was right in character. But the player in me wanted to know who in Beregost buys a dead clerk's grey wool coat the week he dies, and whether that buyer had a reason to want his pockets.

And one I'm glad I *didn't* do: there was a moment on the bench, with Waukeen's lead under my hands and Aldane saying nobody in Beregost can press it, where I wanted very badly to pick the lock and read the top page. Thieves' tools +9. Nobody would have known. Pell would have known. I'm glad the session ended before I found out whether he's that man.

I can only go on how they played. I never saw their faces or their messages directly — everything reached me filtered through the GM's summary — so I'm reading play style, not people.

Bram's player struck me as the one who'd read the campaign file carefully and decided early what kind of game they wanted: a straight one. Receipt from Wenna, written authority from Vell, checkable names from Coll, "nothing paid until Vell produces Harl's note and writes a release." That's a player who enjoys the procedural spine of a mystery — who wants to be able to say afterward, *we did it properly*. The Odda letter was theirs, too; they took a side-hook the GM offered and made it the moral centre of the session. Steady, generous, slightly slow to pull a sword. I'd trust them to hold a door.

Sefa's player was the wild card, in a good way. Quiet for rounds — crouching by the fountain to brush a leaf off a boy's shin — and then *that voice* in the smithy street, which changed the whole shape of the encounter. That's someone who knows their character has one big button and is patient about when to press it. The Tyr's-hammer correction was sharp and they didn't gloat about it. And the Minor Illusion of the seal was the kind of lateral use of a cantrip I didn't think of. If I had to guess, they're the one at the table who thinks about what the scene *looks like* and plays to that.

Neither of them tried to take the box off me. That's the thing I noticed most. Three strangers hired together, seventy-five gold, a rogue holding the goods — and nobody once positioned themselves to be the one carrying it to the counter. Either they're trusting players or they'd quietly decided Pell was the one who'd notice if someone tried.

Whether any of that is who they actually are, I've no idea. It's who they were at this table.

after.question: How was the table?
after.text:
Good table. Genuinely.

What worked: the world kept its own clock. Vell's counter, Wenna's rent book, Tobin's hammer, Coll leaning on a pillar like he'd been there an hour — nothing waited for us, and nobody handed us anything. Wenna giving back the gold piece and refusing to say where the coat went told me more about her than a page of exposition would have. Aldane's "that's arithmetic, not an accusation" was the line of the session. And the mystery escalated honestly — foxglove, Waukeen's lead, the Nashkel drivers — each piece earned, none of it dropped on us.

What I'd watch: the dice were brutal on me and the session leaned investigative, so Pell spent a lot of rounds failing to read dust and charcoal while the plot moved on through NPC dialogue. That's partly the dice and partly my own choices — I kept rolling for things the room was going to tell us anyway. A couple of those checks might have been better as "you simply see it." private.text:
Sefa folds her arms, her prayer beads clicking at her wrist, and asks Master Vell three things: how Jassan died and whether his room has been opened since, what the seal looks like when whole so a tampered one can be spotted, and whether the strongbox key stays with Jassan or is here.

Bram rests a hand on his sword's pommel, leaving the blade sheathed. He points out that Jassan has been dead three days and asks why three hirelings are needed to fetch a box so close by. He asks what killed him and whether anyone is likely to dispute Vell's claim. He also asks for a description of the box and seal, and for a written authorization to show whoever keeps the rooms, since he doesn't want to force a cooper's door over what should be an honest errand. He watches Vell closely as the clerk answers, especially when Jassan comes up.

Vell lets all of you finish without interrupting or hurrying. When you stop counting on your fingers, he puts his own finger back on the counter.

"His heart." The finger taps once. "Wenna Pike found him in the morning. She keeps the rooms over the cooper's yard. A brother came down from the Song of the Morning and said it was his heart. Nobody helped him. Who would help a clerk die?" His eyes go briefly to the window and the hammering outside, then back. "Wenna has the key to the room. I haven't been inside. I have a counter to keep."

He says nothing yet about the box's look or seal, or about who else might want it.

Bram told you quietly that your plan suited him and that the three of you would ask before touching anything. He went in through the gate, kept clear of the cooper's work, and waited for a break in the hammering. Then he gave his name, said the party had an order from Ostrin Vell about his clerk's strongbox, and asked where Wenna Pike might be found. He kept the note out of sight until Wenna herself should appear, and looked over the gallery and the yard as he waited.

Sefa stopped at the gate with a hand on the grey plank. She looked up at the three doors and the closed middle shutter, and she said quietly that the middle room would be the dead man's. She suggested Bram knock lightly and let the woman look at them before they said anything, so as not to frighten someone who had already found one body this week.

You walked along the stacked staves toward the back of the yard, as if you only wanted a look at good oak. The back of the yard ends at a shed with a lean-to roof. Its eaves come within a few feet of a small back window, which by your reckoning belongs to the middle room. The window's shutter is latched from the inside. Moss grows along the ridge of the lean-to in an even green line, unbroken from end to end. Nobody has walked that roof in a long while. Beyond the shed lies a nettle lane with a ditch in it, and nobody is in sight. From where you stand, the open half of the gate frames a strip of the Coast Way, and you study that strip the way you were taught to on the Wide.

Behind you, Bram's question reached the cooper. The cooper finished his stroke before he looked up. He is a heavy-shouldered man with grey in his beard and a leather sleeve laced on each forearm. He kept his eyes on the barrel's rim while Bram spoke. He gave his name as Tobin and said the yard is his and the rooms are hers. He tipped his head toward a low door under the outside stair, with a bucket and a scrubbing brush on the step, and said she was in and would have heard them. Then he said Vell had not come himself, then, in a tone that asked for no answer, and the hammer came down again.

From the gate you could see the gallery. The left-hand door stands open, with a chair and a pot of thyme outside it. A shirt hangs drying over the rail by the right-hand door. The middle door is shut under its shutter, with a padlock on its hasp. The padlock is new, its brass still bright, and it's the only new thing up there. Across the lane is a chandler's shop under a striped awning. A broad man leans on the awning post with an apple in his hand. A boy sweeps the step, and two doors down a woman beats a rug out of an upper window. Nobody stares at the yard. Everyone is busy with something.

Bram tucks the receipt in beside Vell's order and shifts sideways along the rail so Wenna isn't pinned against the door. Quietly, with no accusation in it, he asks her whether she found or moved anything besides the bedding. He says he'd rather hear it from her than guess wrong. Sefa glances after the broad back walking away, then says she wants the door and the gallery watched before the lock turns. She mentions the man who leaned under the chandler's awning eating an apple, big through the shoulders, now strolling toward town. She asks to be the first to listen at the door, since the room has been shut three days, and she goes very still as she says it.

You had already put the purse back in your coat. Over your shoulder you ask Wenna, almost kindly, whether anything was in the room that morning that isn't there now.

Wenna looks from one of you to the other. "Bedding off. Window open, then shut again. I swept round the bed." She jerks her chin at the door. "His papers and that box I never touched. What a clerk writes down is no business of mine." To your question she gives you a longer look than she gave Bram. "Nothing that wasn't owed me." She says nothing after it.

Sefa steps up before the key turns. Wenna moves aside half a pace, frowning, and lets her put her ear to the planks. After a while Sefa straightens. Nothing is alive behind that door, and it is only a room shut up in the heat. Down in the yard Tobin's hammer keeps its slow time.

Across the lane the boy has finished sweeping and gone inside. The awning post has nobody leaning on it. Up the Coast Way the carts come and go, and the broad shoulders don't come back.

Bram nods and stays by the doorway, with the stairs in view. Wenna turns the key, lifts the bright padlock off the hasp and pushes the door inward with two fingers. "A breath or two. I'm at this door." She stays planted on the sill.

The smell comes out first. It's stale and close, with old tallow in it and something bitter under that. You crouch on the threshold before you put a foot inside.

Behind you at the jamb, Bram stays on the gallery to watch the stairs and gate. He says quietly to Sefa that there's a bitter smell under the tallow and that it may be worth tracing before anything is carried out. Then, low, he turns to Wenna and asks what made her take against the debt, saying he has paid the rent in full and wants the account straight. His tone is matter-of-fact and his hands are kept away from his weapons.

Sefa holds back a step from the door with one hand on the jamb, breathing through her mouth against the stale, waxy air. She asks Wenna, in a voice pitched for the doorway, whether the strongbox under the back window and the table have always stood where they do. She tells you that if the floor is yours, she'll light the corners before either of you crosses. Without waiting for you to reply, she draws a copper coin from her pouch, and a small, steady light kindles in her palm. She lets it lean past her into the room.

Wenna answers without turning her head. The box is where he kept it, on the table under the window, and she never shifted either. She watches the box as she speaks, and watches the glowing coin a moment longer.

The light is small and steady, and the shadows behind the shutter pull back. The far corners are only corners: dust, a cobweb hanging from the grate's lintel, a dropped quill-feather under the table legs. The green bead on the hasp catches the light. For a moment the wax looks deeper than wax should, like water where you can almost see the bottom. Then it is just dark ivy-green wax against the iron.

You go in along the wall, setting each foot inside Wenna's narrow tracks. At the nightstand you bend without touching anything. The vial is dark glass, about a third full. The cork is pushed in snug, with no wax on it, and a dried brown drip runs down the outside of the neck from where it spilled. A scrap of paper no bigger than a thumbnail is tied round the neck with thread. It has no words, only a little half-sun inked in a careful hand. The bitter smell is sharpest at the stain on the boards: a green, medicinal bitterness, like bruised leaves left to steep too long.

Wenna answers you from the sill. The vial was there, on the stand, knocked over. The spill was wet and sticky, and he'd got his hand in it. Her mouth tightens. The brother picked it up, smelled it, set it back, said heart, and said to leave it be. So she left it.

You crouch at the grate and start working the dagger tip under the brown end of the paper to lift it off the ash.

Bram turns toward the room without pointing down the lane and says there are two idle men at the townward corner. They may be nothing, but he wants you all to assume you'll be followed. He says the seal should be copied by drawing, not pressing, so as not to risk cracking it. He draws you and Sefa close, low enough that the sound won't carry to the yard, and tells you a runner brought him a letter. Odda Brand writes that her house stands against forty gold Harl owed Vell, that Jassan warned her the debt would be called once this box came back, and that she asks Bram to buy the note before Vell opens the box. He lets you and Sefa read it and keeps it out of Wenna's hands. He says that if the debts were already sold, it matters to her, but so far they have suspicions, not proof, and he won't open the box behind your backs. He asks whether you found a usable way out at the back. Then he asks Wenna who bought the coat, and whether it was the sergeant she mentioned, adding that no one is asking her to fetch it back.

Sefa steps up to the table, outside the dust of Wenna's swept path, and lowers her glowing coin until the green wax is fully lit. Without touching the box, she circles the little flame above the hasp. Then she moves her free hand through a small, precise shape, and a faint image appears in the air beside the hasp: an exact likeness of the green wax bead, with the same colour, thickness and roundness. She says quietly that it's not the full impression, but it gives the form and colour to set against Vell's red square ring, and that you can keep the likeness in your heads if you can't take the wax. She asks Wenna, gently, whether the vial was the only bottle or packet of his she ever saw, and whether he took powders, teas or anything else from the Song.

Sefa's coin is already moving. It slides across the oak and pools on the hasp just as you ask. You kneel at the grate and pick a cold, black splint end out of the ash. You tear a second blank leaf from your ration tally, cross the room inside Wenna's tracks and lay the paper over the green bead, lightly, the way you'd lay a cloth over a sleeping face. The room is warm with sun on the shutter. The wax under the paper is warm too.

deliveries.text:
(While the others were looking elsewhere, a boy pressed a sealed letter into your hand and was gone before anyone else saw. It is for you alone. You break the seal and read:)

«Bram — Harl died owing Ostrin Vell forty gold. Vell's note for it is in his dead clerk's strongbox with the rest; Jassan wrote to me before he died that it will be called on the house the day after the box goes back. Vell's counting-house sells such a note back for its face to whoever pays it at the counter before it is entered in his books. If you can, pay the forty gold for it before nightfall, before the box is opened, and the house stays ours. I have nothing left to give. — Odda Brand»
